item.title: Tanuki: Pon’s Summer review – an adorable raccoon mends the world, one parcel at a time
item.description: Nintendo Switch/2, PlayStation 4/5, Xbox One/series X/S, PC; Denkiworks/Inpleron Limited This gentle game of fixing and fetching, in which you play as a furry post office worker on a BMX, has a slow, calming magic that delights in routine and restoration Arriving alongside November’s blue wave , Tanuki: Pon’s Summer is a game of quiet restoration that feels perfectly suited to the current moment. Tasked with repairing an ancient shrine in the weeks leading up to a local festival, you’ll find yourself cleaning out trash, mending broken arches and slowly bringing a small rural community back together. It sounds a bit like JL Carr’s compact but enchanting novel A Month in the Country , except instead of shell-shocked veterans of the first world war you’re left exploring the rich inner life of a Japanese racoon dog who can ride a BMX. Even so, the mixture of steady progress and general low stakes proves intoxicating. This is a short game, but it’s hard not to linger over it. Continue reading...

item.title: London hotel put admin login for booking website on whiteboard behind the front desk
item.description: Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where all the victims are self-owned. This week, we welcome you to a London hotel where you could check out its admin credentials for a booking website just by walking past the front desk. Our story comes courtesy of Neycho Tepavicharov, co-founder of Flashcloud, a Delaware-based web hosting company. He was staying at a hotel in London when he noticed a shocking breach of basic security protocols by management, who were a little too hospitable with their credentials. As he was passing through the lobby, Tepavicharov noticed that the door behind the front desk was open and, inside that back room, there was a whiteboard. On the whiteboard, written in plain English, were the hotel’s Booking.com administrative username and password. Anyone near the desk could clearly see the login information, and if they didn’t have time to write it down, they could have snapped a picture for later use. As Tepavicharov explains, there’s plenty of mischief you could perform with these credentials. “With that login, someone could change or cancel reservations, see guests’ names and contact details, or message guests pretending to be the hotel,” he said. “Fake 'please confirm your payment' messages sent from compromised hotel accounts are a well-known scam.” An attacker could potentially exploit that access to disrupt hotel operations or target guests with convincing scams. Whether the exposed credentials alone would have been enough to access the account would depend on its security settings. Tepavicharov decided to play the role of good samaritan and warn the hotel’s manager that the business was endangering itself by showing everyone its password. “I asked to speak with the manager and showed him what I’d seen. He was mortified and very grateful,” Tepavicharov said. “Nobody on staff had thought of it as a risk. It was just the easiest way for the whole team to share one login.” After Tepavicharov talked to the manager, not only did the hotel change its ways, but it also moved its website to his hosting service, Flashcloud. Tepavicharov notes that there are plenty of takeaways from this incident. Most important: give each user dedicated credentials with their own separate login, and use multi-factor authentication. “The lesson is an old one, but it keeps happening,” he said. “Shared logins end up written somewhere convenient. Give each staff member their own login, turn on two-factor authentication, and keep passwords in a password manager, not on the wall.” ®

item.title: Data sovereignty takes more than keeping data close to home
item.description: Keeping sensitive data within national borders might satisfy a residency requirement. But does it mean your organization is genuinely in control? Not necessarily. Data could be stored locally while remaining subject to another jurisdiction's laws, dependent on overseas service providers or exposed to disruption beyond your control. For enterprise IT teams, that distinction is becoming harder to ignore. Geopolitical tensions, evolving regulations and the growing use of AI are forcing organizations to reconsider what data sovereignty means in practice. Yet translating those concerns into a workable strategy is another matter. And simply throwing more money at the problem won't necessarily solve it. In The Register's on-demand webinar, Data Sovereignty By Design, moderator Tim Phillips speaks with Patrick Smith, Field CTO for EMEA at Everpure, formerly Pure Storage, about moving beyond compliance checklists and taking a more strategic approach to data control. Drawing on findings from Everpure's research, Smith explores a curious disconnect: organizations are increasing their investment in sovereignty initiatives, yet many still lack a coordinated strategy. Some of the risks attracting the most attention aren't necessarily those receiving the greatest investment. The discussion examines why sovereignty shouldn't be treated as an IT-only responsibility. Decisions about which data needs protection, which services must remain operational and what level of risk is acceptable require input from business leaders, security, procurement and legal teams. There's also the question of priorities. Not every workload needs the same sovereign controls, and attempting to protect everything equally can make an already complicated challenge considerably harder. Smith explains the concept of the "minimum viable company," identifying the critical services, applications and data an organization needs to keep operating through disruption. He also considers why visibility into data access, supplier dependencies and potential exit strategies should influence technology decisions from the outset. For IT leaders trying to turn sovereignty from an abstract boardroom concern into something actionable, the conversation offers useful questions to take back to their organizations. Because knowing where your data sits is one thing. Knowing whether you can maintain control when circumstances change is quite another. Watch the full Data Sovereignty By Design webinar on demand Sponsored by Everpure

item.title: Kerrygold Engages Women in Business and Leadership at 25th WIMBIZ Annual Conference
item.description: Kerrygold strengthened its engagement with consumers and showcased its distinctive dairy offerings at the 25th Women in Management, Business and Public Service (WIMBIZ) Annual Conference, held on November 5 and 6, 2026, at Eko Hotel & Suites, Lagos. The participation provided an opportunity for the renowned Irish dairy brand to connect with an influential audience of women in business, leadership and public service. Through its sponsorship of the conference, Kerrygold aligned with a platform that brings together accomplished women from diverse sectors to share ideas, build networks and explore opportunities for growth. The 25th edition, which celebrated WIMBIZ’s 25-year contribution to women’s empowerment, was themed “ Rooted, Rising, Ready: Born in Africa, Built for the World,” with conversations centred on leadership, business growth and the evolving role of African women in shaping the future. A key highlight of Kerrygold’s participation was its exhibition stand, where attendees had the opportunity to explore the brand’s product range, learn more about its dairy offerings and enjoy product sampling. The stand also provided a welcoming space for direct interactions with guests, allowing them to experience Kerrygold more closely and discover what makes its products distinctive. Beyond showcasing its products, Kerrygold’s presence at the conference reflected its commitment to strengthening brand visibility, building relevance and fostering meaningful consumer relationships. By creating opportunities for attendees to interact with the brand and experience its offerings firsthand, Kerrygold brought its quality and distinctive taste closer to an audience with whom it sought to build lasting connections. As Kerrygold continues to grow its presence in Nigeria, engagements at relevant platforms such as WIMBIZ complement its efforts to introduce more consumers to the brand. Rooted in a rich Irish dairy heritage and celebrated for its distinctive rich, creamy taste, Kerrygold remains focused on creating opportunities for more people to discover and enjoy its quality dairy products. Sponsored Content The post Kerrygold Engages Women in Business and Leadership at 25th WIMBIZ Annual Conference appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: Your AI agent is only as good as your endpoint data
item.description: Every so often a flaw comes along that shows how fast the ground can shift under IT and security teams. PHP2Shell, a pair of critical flaws in PHP, was one of them. Details leaked before the planned disclosure, frontier AI helped researchers find the flaws, and PHP shipped fixes the next day. For many teams, though, the patch was the easy part. So what does it take to respond at that speed, and where should teams begin? What does governed autonomous IT look like in practice? Picture a loop. Software finds where a risk lives and ranks what matters most. It proposes a fix, then, inside limits people define, carries it out and checks that it worked. Routine, low-risk actions can run on their own. Higher-impact ones wait for a person to approve. A few are never handed over at all. Each step leaves a record that someone can review and reverse. What challenges do IT and security teams face today? Three problems keep coming up. The first is visibility. PHP2Shell reportedly sat undetected for more than a decade. For these two flaws, the fix was a version upgrade. The hard part was finding every copy of PHP, including copies bundled inside other software or extracted by hand onto Windows machines that never registered as installed applications. Then teams had to work out which copies the internet could reach and check for signs of earlier attack. An inventory built from a periodic snapshot can't answer those questions on the day they matter. The second is tool-hopping. Answering "where does this run, and can the internet reach it?" often means pivoting across an asset inventory, a vulnerability scanner and an external attack surface tool, each with its own view. Every hop adds delay. Every console is another chance to disagree with the last. The third is pace. Several security firms reported exploitation attempts before PHP released its fixes, and Cloudflare reported early attacks hours ahead of the patch. Frontier AI models helped find PHP2Shell, and in April Anthropic said its Claude Mythos Preview model had found thousands of previously unknown flaws across every major operating system and browser. With models like these in the picture, the old rhythm of disclose, patch and verify assumes a gap that keeps shrinking. Put an AI agent on top of stale, fragmented data and these problems don't go away. They scale. Why does real-time endpoint data make autonomy trustworthy? Endpoints are where work happens and where many attacks end up, so they are the ground truth for any decision about the estate. Four qualities make that data a sound foundation for autonomous action: Accuracy: Live data from the endpoints themselves, not a snapshot that was true last week. Speed: A short path from question to action, with no hopping between tools to reconcile answers. Control: Approvals and an audit trail, plus the ability to roll back, so any automated action can be reviewed and reversed. item.dc:creator: Tanium
item.content:encoded: Every so often a flaw comes along that shows how fast the ground can shift under IT and security teams. PHP2Shell, a pair of critical flaws in PHP, was one of them. Details leaked before the planned disclosure, frontier AI helped researchers find the flaws, and PHP shipped fixes the next day. For many teams, though, the patch was the easy part. So what does it take to respond at that speed, and where should teams begin? What does governed autonomous IT look like in practice? Picture a loop. Software finds where a risk lives and ranks what matters most. It proposes a fix, then, inside limits people define, carries it out and checks that it worked. Routine, low-risk actions can run on their own. Higher-impact ones wait for a person to approve. A few are never handed over at all. Each step leaves a record that someone can review and reverse. What challenges do IT and security teams face today? Three problems keep coming up. The first is visibility. PHP2Shell reportedly sat undetected for more than a decade. For these two flaws, the fix was a version upgrade. The hard part was finding every copy of PHP, including copies bundled inside other software or extracted by hand onto Windows machines that never registered as installed applications. Then teams had to work out which copies the internet could reach and check for signs of earlier attack. An inventory built from a periodic snapshot can't answer those questions on the day they matter. The second is tool-hopping. Answering "where does this run, and can the internet reach it?" often means pivoting across an asset inventory, a vulnerability scanner and an external attack surface tool, each with its own view. Every hop adds delay. Every console is another chance to disagree with the last. The third is pace. Several security firms reported exploitation attempts before PHP released its fixes, and Cloudflare reported early attacks hours ahead of the patch. Frontier AI models helped find PHP2Shell, and in April Anthropic said its Claude Mythos Preview model had found thousands of previously unknown flaws across every major operating system and browser. With models like these in the picture, the old rhythm of disclose, patch and verify assumes a gap that keeps shrinking. Put an AI agent on top of stale, fragmented data and these problems don't go away. They scale. Why does real-time endpoint data make autonomy trustworthy? Endpoints are where work happens and where many attacks end up, so they are the ground truth for any decision about the estate. Four qualities make that data a sound foundation for autonomous action: Accuracy: Live data from the endpoints themselves, not a snapshot that was true last week. Speed: A short path from question to action, with no hopping between tools to reconcile answers. Control: Approvals and an audit trail, plus the ability to roll back, so any automated action can be reviewed and reversed. Shared truth: IT operations, security and the system of record working from one view, rather than arguing over whose data is right. Matt Psencik, a threat research engineer at Tanium, put the visibility problem bluntly when PHP2Shell broke: "The installations that worry me most are the ones a security team doesn't know it owns." How does AI fit in? AI sits on both sides of this. It helped researchers find the PHP2Shell flaws, and attackers can use it to build exploits too. For defenders, AI works best as the operator and the interface: it takes a plain-language question, works out what to ask of the data, and proposes or carries out the next step. But it is only as good as the data it is grounded in. A fluent answer built on outdated information is still wrong, just more confidently so. Keeping people in the loop where stakes are high is what makes automation safe to expand. What are the practical first steps? Teams don't need to hand over the keys all at once. Start here: Find every copy: Don't stop at the installed-applications list. PHP2Shell showed that software bundled inside other products can slip past it. Compare your CMDB against what is really on your network and record exact versions. Draw the lines: Rank systems by what the internet can reach, then decide which response actions run automatically, which need approval and which are never delegated. Write it down before an agent needs it. Pilot one low-risk workflow: Pick something contained, build approval into it, and read the audit trail before widening the scope. Teams can also shorten the pilot with a partner. World Wide Technology (WWT), a Tanium partner, works with many large organizations on technology rollouts and hosts a Tanium lab in its Advanced Technology Center, where customers can test an approach hands-on before moving it into production. That second problem, the hopping, is the one Tanium Atlas was built to close. Instead of moving between consoles, an operator asks a plain-language question, gets an answer from live endpoint data, and acts on it inside limits the team sets, with every action recorded. Want to see how it works in practice? Click here and set up time to see Tanium in action. Sponsored by Tanium.

item.title: Harry Kane’s England caps record: an illustrious career in numbers and charts
item.description: Striker to play historic 126th match and that’s far from the only statistic that sets him apart for his country Harry Kane will become the most capped player for England’s men when he features against Croatia at Wembley. Yet in the context of the grand history of international football, his record total will be relatively low. Kane will draw level with players including Dani Alves, Eden Hazard and Paolo Maldini on 126 caps. Illustrious players, none of whom lead their country’s appearance standings. Neither do Kevin De Bruyne or Luís Figo, on 127, or Manuel Neuer with 128. It will be some time next year before England’s captain enters European football’s top 50 players for international caps, never mind the global standings. Continue reading...

item.title: Less drama, more listening, but is Kozo Tashima the candidate to topple Infantino?
item.description: Japan FA honorary president is hoping a calmer approach that makes fewer unwelcome headlines for Fifa will be welcomed by football Not many remember Japan’s bid for the 2022 World Cup, when the country finished the race with only two of the final 22 votes. Kozo Tashima was involved then, and now the honorary president of the Japan Football Association is going it alone in the hope of ousting Gianni Infantino. The 68-year-old Tashima is an unlikely insurgent and an unlikely challenger to Infantino. He is, however, a familiar and respected figure in Asian and global football politics, and ready to take the Fifa presidency out of the headlines into a quieter era. Continue reading...

The meeting marks ⁠a sharp shift from Sunday, when Nvidia’s board ​expressed confidence in Huang and his leadership team. However, Huang’s position became more tenuous late on Wednesday after it was reported by the New York Times that Huang had a separate extramarital affair with a company employee named Kimberly Powell. She was Nvidia’s president of healthcare and was reportedly captured on video being affectionate with Huang at a hotel during a company conference in March. Continue reading...

item.title: Clint Eastwood's Legendary Western Sequel Is Waiting to Be Discovered on Streaming
item.description: In 1964, Italian director Sergio Leone redefined the Western movie genre with A Fistful of Dollars . Eschewing the relatively simplistic morality tales of earlier films, Leone’s protagonist wasn’t a noble hero, but an opportunistic gunslinger who pits two rival Old West gangs against each other to score a big payday. Despite the moral complexity of it all — or, more likely, because of it — A Fistful of Dollars was an international success that proved three things: audiences were ready for a new kind of Western, America no longer had a monopoly on the genre, and Clint Eastwood was a bankable movie star.

item.title: AWS distills its cloud into a local emulator that runs on your PC
item.description: AWS has released an emulator that kind-of-almost lets you use its cloud on a PC. As explained in the GitHub repository for the prosaically named “AWS Emulator,” the tool “is a local program that serves an AWS API endpoint.” The emulator doesn’t replicate the whole AWS cloud, instead offering its APIs. “You use it to test your software without calling AWS, on your own machine, on a development server, or in continuous integration (CI),” the repo explains. Because those tests never touch the AWS cloud, the tool is free to use. AWS wrote the emulator in Rust, a choice that senior specialist solutions architect Daniel Abib wrote helps to ensure the tool “stays light on CPU and memory on a laptop.” The emulator tool doesn’t replicate the entire AWS cloud. Abib said it supports the APIs of AWS services that have an API model in the AWS API models repository on GitHub . The Register found over 1,300 items on that page. While the tool lets developers test APIs, it doesn’t replicate anywhere near all the features of the Amazonian cloud. “It doesn’t evaluate IAM [Identity and Access Management] policies the way AWS does, and each emulator acts as a single account, with no cross-account or cross-Region behavior,” Abib wrote, adding “How closely it matches AWS varies by service and feature.” AWS publishes “fidelity scores” that detail how closely the emulator works on different AWS services. Amazon tries to achieve full fidelity, so the emulator produces the same results as AWS for valid API calls, and the same errors for invalid ones. Coding agents can also drive the Emulator, an option The Register mentions because AWS advises the easiest way to check if a project will work with the tool is to use the aws-emulator skill for AI coding agents. “With the skill, your agent finds the AWS operations and resources that your project depends on. It checks them against the fidelity tests and fidelity scores for the emulator. It then tells you which parts of your project you can rely on the emulator for, and which ones might behave differently from AWS,” according to AWS documentation. AWS has made the emulator available as an RPM or Debian package. Mac and PC users will need to run Docker and an image of the Emulator. “You install the emulator, start it, and point your tools at the local endpoint,” Abib instructed. “When AWS Emulator starts, it generates its own credentials, a config file, and a certificate, and writes them to ~/.aws/emulator/9297/ . You set environment variables so the AWS SDK talks to your laptop instead of AWS, and your application code stays unchanged.” “From there, your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do. item.content:encoded: AWS has released an emulator that kind-of-almost lets you use its cloud on a PC. As explained in the GitHub repository for the prosaically named “AWS Emulator,” the tool “is a local program that serves an AWS API endpoint.” The emulator doesn’t replicate the whole AWS cloud, instead offering its APIs. “You use it to test your software without calling AWS, on your own machine, on a development server, or in continuous integration (CI),” the repo explains. Because those tests never touch the AWS cloud, the tool is free to use. AWS wrote the emulator in Rust, a choice that senior specialist solutions architect Daniel Abib wrote helps to ensure the tool “stays light on CPU and memory on a laptop.” The emulator tool doesn’t replicate the entire AWS cloud. Abib said it supports the APIs of AWS services that have an API model in the AWS API models repository on GitHub . The Register found over 1,300 items on that page. While the tool lets developers test APIs, it doesn’t replicate anywhere near all the features of the Amazonian cloud. “It doesn’t evaluate IAM [Identity and Access Management] policies the way AWS does, and each emulator acts as a single account, with no cross-account or cross-Region behavior,” Abib wrote, adding “How closely it matches AWS varies by service and feature.” AWS publishes “fidelity scores” that detail how closely the emulator works on different AWS services. Amazon tries to achieve full fidelity, so the emulator produces the same results as AWS for valid API calls, and the same errors for invalid ones. Coding agents can also drive the Emulator, an option The Register mentions because AWS advises the easiest way to check if a project will work with the tool is to use the aws-emulator skill for AI coding agents. “With the skill, your agent finds the AWS operations and resources that your project depends on. It checks them against the fidelity tests and fidelity scores for the emulator. It then tells you which parts of your project you can rely on the emulator for, and which ones might behave differently from AWS,” according to AWS documentation. AWS has made the emulator available as an RPM or Debian package. Mac and PC users will need to run Docker and an image of the Emulator. “You install the emulator, start it, and point your tools at the local endpoint,” Abib instructed. “When AWS Emulator starts, it generates its own credentials, a config file, and a certificate, and writes them to ~/.aws/emulator/9297/ . You set environment variables so the AWS SDK talks to your laptop instead of AWS, and your application code stays unchanged.” “From there, your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do. A unit test that creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back is the same test, and it runs on your machine without a deployment.” The cloud colossus’s intent appears, as ever, to encourage more use of its cloud – in this case by satisfying developers their code will run well when deployed there, and making it easy for them to test for that. ®

item.title: SpaceX launches 2nd mystery mission for US Space Force in 6-day span (video, photos)
item.description: null SpaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force from California tonight (Nov. 11), the second such flight for the company in a six-day span. A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from California's Vandenberg Space Force Base tonight at 11:36 p.m. EST (8:36 p.m. local California time; 0136 GMT on Nov. 12), kicking off a mission called USSF-627. Vandenberg hosted a similar liftoff less than a week ago: On Nov. 6, a Falcon 9 sent the USSF-432 mission skyward from the site, which lies on California's gorgeous but often foggy central coast. A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket launches the USSF-627 mission for the U.S. Space Force from California on Nov. 11, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX) We don't know much about USSF-627 or USSF-432; both are classified. Some experts have speculated , however, that each mission launched a batch of SpaceX's Starshield satellites for the Space Force's Space Based Sensing and Targeting portfolio, which helps the military branch track potential targets around the world. SpaceX didn't reveal details about either USSF-627 or USSF-432, and the company ended the webcast of both launches shortly after the first stages of their Falcon 9 rockets came back to Earth . In both cases, that touchdown occurred about 8.5 minutes after liftoff on the SpaceX droneship "Of Course I Still Love You," which was stationed downrange of Vandenberg in the Pacific Ocean. It was the seventh mission for USSF-627's Falcon 9 booster, which carries the designation 1103. A Falcon 9 first stage rests on a SpaceX drone ship shortly after launching the USSF-627 mission on Nov. 11, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX) Previous Booster 1103 missions NROL-179 | SDA-T1TL-E | SDA-T1TL-A | 3 Starlink missions USSF-627 was the 120th Falcon 9 launch of 2026 and the rocket's 15th national-security flight of the year to date. Eighty-five of the 120 flights have been devoted to building out SpaceX's Starlink broadband constellation in low Earth orbit , which currently consists of more than 11,000 satellites. The Falcon 9 is not on a record-breaking cadence this year. In 2025, the rocket flew a whopping 165 missions , and 122 of them were Starlink flights.

item.title: APOD: 2026 November 12 – Moon, Venus and Spica Meet
item.description: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 12 –… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Moon, Venus and Spica Meet Explanation: Not all those who wander are lost. A night sky example is that planets wander, and in fact the very word “planet” comes from “wandering star” in Greek. As planets shift relative to fixed stars , they may appear from our perspective to get closer to other astronomical objects. Such meetings are called conjunctions . They don’t happen by chance, but follow the precise laws of celestial mechanics . This peaceful image , captured in Poland , shows the crescent Moon above the Tatra Mountains , and bright Venus close by, a little lower in the horizon. The bright star to the left of Venus is Spica in the constellation of Virgo , the Maiden. Spica is one of the brightest stars in the sky, only about 250 light-years away. It was found in 1890 that Spica is a binary star: two massive blue stars orbiting each other every 4 days. But earlier this year it was reported that Spica, the current companion of wandering Venus, is actually a triple system . Tomorrow’s picture: what’s next? Date November 12, 2026 Credit & Copyright Włodzimierz Bubak Authors & editors: Cecilia Chirenti, Robert Nemiroff, Jerry Bonnell, Keighley Rockcliffe A service of: ASD at NASA / GSFC , NASA Science Activation & Michigan Tech. item.title: Scotland’s Flow Country
item.description: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory Scotland’s Flow Country Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search March 4, 2024 Compared to ecosystems in many other parts of the world, the blanket bogs of the Flow Country in northern Scotland are unassuming—soggy, treeless landscapes dominated by hummocky mosses, grasses, and heathers. Yet, to ecologists, the seemingly desolate areas are nothing short of extraordinary. The bogs store tremendous quantities of carbon . That’s because their soils are so waterlogged that microbes cannot fully break down dead plant material, a process that would otherwise release carbon dioxide. Instead, partially decayed plant matter accumulates into thick layers of spongy, crumbly, carbon-rich material called peat . The unusual ecosystems, also called blanket mires and featherbed bogs, only occur in places with abundant rainfall, poor drainage, and low levels of evapotranspiration . These types of bogs cover just 120,000 square kilometers (46,000 square miles) globally, less than one-tenth of one percent of Earth’s land surface. The image above, captured by the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 8 , is centered on blanket bogs in the Scottish Highlands, home to the largest such ecosystem in Europe. This peatland is also the first of its type to be inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site . The peat bogs of northern Scotland, home to more than 30 species of sphagnum moss , are spread across some 1,900 square kilometers (730 square miles) of the country’s Highlands region. In this image, boggy areas appear dark brown and are sprinkled with lakes. The light green area on the right side around Thurso is farmland. The darker green geometric patterns in the center are conifer plantations . The image was captured in the spring, the part of the year when the land surface is most waterlogged and peat bogs begin to accumulate large amounts of new biomass. While forests store most of their carbon in living trees—which eventually release it back into the atmosphere when they burn or die—peat bogs often store carbon for many thousands of years. Some parts of the Flow Country have been accumulating peat for more than 9,000 years, building deposits exceeding eight meters thick, according to UNESCO. Overall, scientists estimate that all of the world’s peatlands cover just 3 percent of Earth’s land surface but store more than 600 gigatons of carbon—about twice as much as all the world’s forests combined. NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey . Story by Adam Voiland. Downloads March 4, 2024 JPEG (7.52 MB) References & Resources Aitke

item.title: Disgraced former CA eMudhra blames buggy script for hopelessly weak certificates
item.description: Former certification authority eMudhra has claimed a buggy Python script is the main reason it issued laughably insecure digital certificates. The company posted its account of the matter on Bugzilla where a user with the handle “Naveen Kumar ML” wrote “During a single key‑generation ceremony on 30 April 2025, sixteen subordinate (issuing) CA key pairs in eMudhra’s ‘B’ and ‘C’ series were generated correctly on a hardware security module and then processed through an approved wrap/unwrap round‑trip using a custom python key‑handling script.” eMudhra aimed to create eight ECDSA P-384 private keys which should have been 48 bytes long. But the script contained what Kumar described as “a bug/defect in the import code [which] resulted in a read‑back from the unwrapped object that truncated the private value, so the certified public keys correspond to private scalars below the expected range and are recoverable from public information.” The truncation is the key problem here, because it appears that eMudhra ignored 47 of the 48 bytes, producing its infamously insecure single-byte keys such as the number four. Whatever the nature of the bug, Kumar asserts it was “a custom script run only on an isolated ceremony host and was not a function of the emCA software.” eMudhra needed that script because “global supply chain constraints” meant it couldn’t acquire the hardware security modules (HSMs), devices that generate and store cryptographic keys, that it wanted to use when creating a set of certificates for use in the USA. It therefore used HSMs made by a company called Utimaco to generate keys and planned to transfer the keys it produced to a different set of HSMs from a company called Crypto4A. Kumar explained that eMudhra decided on that move, which is unusual, because changes to policy about provenance of certificates meant it had to generate new certs by the end of May. The plan went sour when the company didn’t notice the errors in its script and didn’t test the keys it created. The rest is history: a Mozilla team member noticed that the company’s keys were woefully weak and pointed out that attackers could therefore issue fraudulent certificates that allowed them to impersonate servers, observe traffic, or even modify data in transit. Browser-makers quickly tweaked their software so it would not recognize certs from eMudhra. The Indian business then quit the SSL/TLS certification business, which it said was never a major source of revenue but had suddenly become a severe source of embarrassment. Kumar’s new post lists three steps eMudhra will take to wind up its certification business, one of which will see the company “Put in place improvements motivated by findings of [an] independent review to strengthen our general PKI operations.” Sounds like a plan. ®

item.title: ACF crisis deepens
item.description: Moves to resolve the lingering supremacy battle within the ranks of the Arewa Consultative Forum (ACF) have yet to produce results after a closed-door meeting by members of the Board of Trustees (BoT), the National Executive Committee (NEC) and some first-class emirs from the northern region ended in what some sources described as “deadlock.” Daily Trust learnt that the meeting, which took place on Tuesday at the private residence of the Sultan of Sokoto, Alhaji Muhammadu Sa’ad Abubakar III, in Maitama, Abuja, lasted two hours between 5pm and 7pm without any tangible resolutions reached. The traditional rulers at the meeting included the Etsu Nupe, Alhaji Yahaya Abubakar, and the Aku Uka of Wukari, Dr. Manu Ishaku Adda Ali. The Sultan was reportedly not at the meeting as he was attending to other matters of national importance somewhere. Although the details of the meeting, which was convened at the instance of the Sultan, were sketchy, sources privy to the happenings in the ACF confided in Daily Trust that the gathering focused on resolving the worsening division in the leadership of the northern socio-political group. One of the sources said both the Etsu Nupe and the Aku Uka expressed serious reservations over the inability of the BoT and NEC to arrive at a neutral ground and work together towards finding solution to the security and economic challenges afflicting the North. “In fact, one of the emirs alluded to the fact that the North is now a laughing stock…That we cannot speak with one voice at a critical moment of our existence,” he said. Our correspondents report that the meeting on Tuesday was a continuation of series of engagements with contending parties (NEC and BoT) towards resolving the protracted leadership crisis occasioned by alleged financial impropriety. Daily Trust learnt that the Sultan, with the support of the Emir of Lafia, Justice Sidi Dauda Bage Muhammad and other northern traditional rulers have been having talks with the ACF leaders since the beginning of 2026 when the BoT and NEC engaged in blame game. On one hand, the Chairman of the BoT, Alhaji Bashir Dalhatu, with the support of some members, had asked the Secretary General of the organisation, Malam Murtala Aliyu, to leave. But Murtala had kicked saying his tenure will expire in December 2026. He reportedly has the support of some members, including the Chairman of the NEC, Barrister Mamman Mike Osuman, SAN. Besides the leadership tussle, the lodgement of about N3.9 billion donated to the ACP in a new account at JAIZ Bank, rather than in any of the main accounts of the organisation in First Bank, United Bank for Africa (UBA) and Unity Bank, has caused disaffection among members. During its 25th anniversary celebration held in November 2025, some notable northern leaders and businessmen donated the amount, in addition to pledges that are yet to be redeemed. Also, there was nearly N700 million donated by some northern leaders in order to organise the 25th anniversary

Although the details of the meeting, which was convened at the instance of the Sultan, were sketchy, sources privy to the happenings in the ACF confided in Daily Trust that the gathering focused on resolving the worsening division in the leadership of the northern socio-political group. One of the sources said both the Etsu Nupe and the Aku Uka expressed serious reservations over the inability of the BoT and NEC to arrive at a neutral ground and work together towards finding solution to the security and economic challenges afflicting the North. “In fact, one of the emirs alluded to the fact that the North is now a laughing stock…That we cannot speak with one voice at a critical moment of our existence,” he said. Our correspondents report that the meeting on Tuesday was a continuation of series of engagements with contending parties (NEC and BoT) towards resolving the protracted leadership crisis occasioned by alleged financial impropriety. Daily Trust learnt that the Sultan, with the support of the Emir of Lafia, Justice Sidi Dauda Bage Muhammad and other northern traditional rulers have been having talks with the ACF leaders since the beginning of 2026 when the BoT and NEC engaged in blame game. On one hand, the Chairman of the BoT, Alhaji Bashir Dalhatu, with the support of some members, had asked the Secretary General of the organisation, Malam Murtala Aliyu, to leave. But Murtala had kicked saying his tenure will expire in December 2026. He reportedly has the support of some members, including the Chairman of the NEC, Barrister Mamman Mike Osuman, SAN. Besides the leadership tussle, the lodgement of about N3.9 billion donated to the ACP in a new account at JAIZ Bank, rather than in any of the main accounts of the organisation in First Bank, United Bank for Africa (UBA) and Unity Bank, has caused disaffection among members. During its 25th anniversary celebration held in November 2025, some notable northern leaders and businessmen donated the amount, in addition to pledges that are yet to be redeemed. Also, there was nearly N700 million donated by some northern leaders in order to organise the 25th anniversary. Details of how the funds were utilised are being questioned. Established in the year 2000, the ACF, a socio-cultural organisation which draws its membership from the 19 northern states, seeks to protect the interests of Northern Nigeria. The recent role of the traditional rulers in finding a lasting solution reportedly followed the intervention of Vice President Kashim Shettima, who had earlier formed a committee of eminent northern leaders to resolve the crisis. It was learnt that Shettima’s intervention also followed a call by former Heads of State who are the patrons of the ACF. Those who attended the Tuesday meeting with the Etsu Nupe and the Aku Uka included Alhaji Yayale Ahmed, Malam Gambo Hamza, Professor Tijjani Bande, Alhaji Bashir Dalhatu, Mr Mamman Mike Osuman, SAN, and Professor Muhammad Tukur, among others. But the secretary general, Aliyu, was not at the meeting. When contacted last night, he confirmed that he did not attend the meeting. “The police had invited me for an interaction around the time of the meeting. This is the reason I didn’t go to the Sultan’s house,” he said. Another source said he would not describe the Tuesday meeting as “stalemate” because it continued yesterday (Wednesday). The source, who said the root of the crisis is ego, added that he was optimistic the problem will be resolved. “Posterity will not judge us positively if all the people that are involve in resolving the crisis failed to achieve the stated goal. I assure you that we will succeed,” he said. ACF secretariat shut The police had on Monday shut down the ACF secretariat in Kaduna, Daily Trust reports. However, there is conflicting report on what actually transpired. A source from the BoT, led by Alhaji Bashir Dalhatu, alleged that it was the NEC, under Mamman Mike Osuman (SAN), that first shut the secretariat. He said this was ahead of their planned meeting today (Thursday). “We have issued a notice of meeting when we discovered that the secretariat had been shut in order to sabotage the meeting,” the source said. But a source from the Osuman faction alleged that the Bashir Dalhatu led officials forced their way into offices and replaced the locks, including those of the mosque within the premises. Meanwhile, staff members of the forum have been directed by the management to stay away from the secretariat for one week, starting from Monday, as the crisis festers. A source at the secretariat, who spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorised to speak to journalists, said the decision followed the invitation of three ACF staff members, including the treasurer, by the police on November 5. The source said the officials were taken to Abuja for questioning, made to write statements and later released on self-recognizance. “For your information, the police came to the office on November 5 and took away the staff members, including the forum’s treasurer, to Abuja for questioning. They were later released after writing their statements. “It was in view of this that the management decided that all staff at the secretariat should stay away from work for one week. We are expected to resume next week,” he said. During a visit to the secretariat along Sokoto Road on Tuesday, our correspondent sighted some policemen at the entrance as the gate remained locked. Bukar Zarma, a senior member of the forum aligned with the Dalhatu faction, confirmed to one of our correspondents that the locks were changed, but defended the action, saying it was necessary to enable the BoT to access the premises and hold its scheduled meeting. Zarma alleged that the secretary-general under the Osuman faction, Murtala Aliyu had locked the secretariat and directed workers to stay away to prevent the trustees from holding their meeting. “We went to the secretariat at about 11am on Monday. The Board of Trustees had issued a notice of a meeting scheduled to take place sometime this week. However, in reaction to the notice, the secretary-general ordered the closure of the secretariat to prevent the Board of Trustees from holding its meeting,” he said. Zarma alleged that the secretary-general not only locked the premises but also sent the workers away and secured virtually every part of the building, including the toilets. He further claimed that the staff were instructed not to respond to calls from members of the BoT, while attempts to reach the secretary-general were unsuccessful. According to him, the trustees reported the matter to the police and requested security assistance to gain access to the building. He maintained that the ACF secretariat and other assets of the organisation were under the custody of the BoT and not the secretary-general. “How can somebody who is, so to speak, a tenant lock out the landlord from the property? The secretariat does not belong to the secretary-general; it belongs to the organisation and its members,” he said. Zarma said police personnel accompanie

item.title: Russian cloud Yandex says drone attacks on its datacenters caused data loss
item.description: Russian cloud operator Yandex has admitted to data loss after a drone attack on one of its datacenters. The attack, which Ukrainian press said was ordered by Kyiv, happened in early October and caused a fire and subsequent outage at Yandex’s ru-central1-b availability zone. Subsequent strikes targeted more Yandex datacenters and disrupted more of the company’s cloud and payment services. On Tuesday, Yandex posted an update on its recovery efforts, which it spun as something of a triumph because it restored over 97 percent of customer data. Of course that also means the company lost 2.84 percent of customer data, which it blamed on “critical hardware damage and a lack of backups on the platform.” It’s unclear if Yandex’s use of the phrase “on the platform” indicates it doesn’t keep backups of its own cloud, if whatever resilience techniques it employs don’t create multiple copies of customer data, or if clients didn’t protect their data. Whatever happened, Yandex has decided to enable backups by default for all VMs customers create in its cloud. That decision will mean customers will consume and pay for more Yandex resources, unless they opt out of the automated backups. Given that drones damaged three Yandex locations, and the war with Ukraine continues, users have good reasons to consider alternatives to its services. Indeed, Yandex’s announcement of its recovery efforts links to a page extolling the virtues of a hybrid cloud when devising data protection strategies. That page also mentions Yandex’s own Stackland product, which brings its stack on-prem, as an example of a hybrid approach. On Wednesday the company also launched a new availability zone named ru-central1-f. Yandex didn’t say where it’s located, other than to say it’s in “a new location.” Interestingly, Yandex has imposed quotas that limit the amount of resources users can access in the new availability zone and says it can’t yet handle traffic to private endpoints at the new facility. Many nations have imposed sanctions that restrict sales of technology products to Russia. It’s therefore unsurprising that Yandex might struggle to provision enough infrastructure to allow untrammeled access to a new availability zone. ®

item.title: Curiosity Blog, Sols 5063-5069 Rocks and Chips
item.description: Curiosity Navigation Curiosity Home Mission Overview Where is Curiosity? Mission Updates Science Overview Instruments Highlights Exploration Goals News and Features Multimedia Curiosity Raw Images Images Videos Audio Mosaics More Resources Mars Missions Mars Perseverance Rover Mars Curiosity Rover Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter Mars Odyssey More Mars Missions Mars Home 2 min read Curiosity Blog, Sols 5063-5069 Rocks and Chips NASA’s Mars rover Curiosity acquired this image of chip-shaped crystal forms using its Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI), located on the turret at the end of the rover’s robotic arm, on November 7, 2026, Sol 5067 of the Mars Science Laboratory Mission, at 14:07:35 UTC. NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS Written by William Farrand, Senior Research Scientist, Space Science Institute Earth planning date: Friday, Nov. 6, 2026 This week Curiosity has been completing its drill campaign at the “Nazca” drill hole. This is an area characterized by bedrock containing disk-shaped (or in a liberal interpretation, potato chip shaped … see linked image) crystal forms. A key objective has been to better characterize these chip-shaped features. Drill samples were delivered to the Sample Analysis for Mars (SAM) instrument. While the SAM analysis was on-going, Monday’s plan included a ChemCam LIBS observation of another crystal-form, “Ahi Veremos,” more Mastcam frames to fill out a mosaic of the Nazca near to mid-field, and environmental observations including a large dust devil survey, and horizon and atmospheric zenith movies. Wednesday’s plan included two targeted science blocks with a LIBS depth profile of the “Colca” crystal-form and LIBS of the “Bermejo ” target. A long distance Remote Micro-Imager (RMI) mosaic of rock clusters below the “Cordillera” ridge was also collected. Mastcam collected more frames of its Nazca mosaic, and more environmental observations were made. Friday’s planning was for three sols with three targeted science blocks and a drive away from the Nazca drill site. A MAHLI mosaic of the side of the block that hosts the Nazca drill hole was planned. It was also planned to use MAHLI’s nighttime white-light and ultraviolet LED lamps for nighttime imaging of the crystal-forms. Mars’ moon, Phobos, was eclipsing the Sun and imaging of that event was prioritized. ChemCam LIBS observations were planned for each sol including a cluster of crystal forms, a resistant layer in the side of the Nazca block and a dark float rock. A long distance RMI mosaic of dark lenses beneath a planar surface on the “Mishe Mokwa” ridge was to be made. Another round of environmental observation was also planned. Finally, Friday’s drive was to take the rover back towards its southerly trending route where Curiosity would continue its trek of exploration and discovery. item.title: Some PFAS chemicals are declining in English rivers but others are appearing
item.description: The River Wye in Derbyshire, England Dave Porter/Alamy The concentration of two of the most well-studied PFAS forever chemicals are showing a strong downward trend in English rivers. The finding adds to a mixed story for the power of global restrictions. The levels of perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS) and perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) in English rivers have fallen by 30 per cent and 29 per cent, respectively, over the past decade, according to a new report by scientists at the Environment Agency (EA) , a UK government green regulator. Both of these human-made chemicals take a long time to break down in the environment. The International Agency for Research on Cancer recently designated PFOA as carcinogenic to humans , and both forever chemicals have been linked to reproductive health and developmental impacts as well as other serious health issues. Advertisement Read more Fish-based pet food may expose cats and dogs to forever chemicals Under the United Nations Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants, the use of PFOS was restricted from 2009, and the use of PFOA was restricted from 2019 – although there were country-specific caveats on which uses they applied to. They had both been used in non-stick coatings on consumer products as well as in industrial processes. Both were also used in firefighting foams, a major source of PFAS pollution entering the environment, with a ban on PFOA in firefighting foams only coming into force in the UK in 2025. Rob Bradburne , the EA’s chief scientist, describes his group’s results as proof that the global ban was “a really positive move”. But, he adds that the huge range of PFAS chemicals is going to “complicate the story”. An issue that is clear in the dataset for England is that while these two main PFAS have declined, many other “forever chemicals” that are being used to replace them – such as short-chain PFAS and fluorotelomer compounds – have now emerged in the environment at detectable levels. Free newsletter Sign up to The Earth Edition Sign up to newsletter There are around 10,000 chemicals defined as PFAS, and they are used in a huge range of products and processes, from cosmetics to industrial lubricants. But the health and environmental impacts of many of these chemicals are relatively understudied. One of the short-chain PFAS that is now particularly widespread across the world is trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) – which can form when pesticides, refrigerants and pharmaceuticals break down in the environment. The EA report confirmed that TFA is widespread in England, and a separate study published this week confirmed that it is also widespread across the UK more generally. “These findings add to the growing weight of evidence that PFAS pollution must be tackled at source if we are to protect our environment and our health,” says Hannah Evans , who worked on this second study and works with the UK environmental charity Fidra. “Other countries are already progressing towards this end… The UK

item.content:encoded: The River Wye in Derbyshire, England Dave Porter/Alamy The concentration of two of the most well-studied PFAS forever chemicals are showing a strong downward trend in English rivers. Both of these human-made chemicals take a long time to break down in the environment. The International Agency for Research on Cancer recently designated PFOA as carcinogenic to humans , and both forever chemicals have been linked to reproductive health and developmental impacts as well as other serious health issues. Advertisement Read more Fish-based pet food may expose cats and dogs to forever chemicals Under the United Nations Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants, the use of PFOS was restricted from 2009, and the use of PFOA was restricted from 2019 – although there were country-specific caveats on which uses they applied to. Both were also used in firefighting foams, a major source of PFAS pollution entering the environment, with a ban on PFOA in firefighting foams only coming into force in the UK in 2025. Rob Bradburne , the EA’s chief scientist, describes his group’s results as proof that the global ban was “a really positive move”. But, he adds that the huge range of PFAS chemicals is going to “complicate the story”. An issue that is clear in the dataset for England is that while these two main PFAS have declined, many other “forever chemicals” that are being used to replace them – such as short-chain PFAS and fluorotelomer compounds – have now emerged in the environment at detectable levels. Free newsletter Sign up to The Earth Edition Sign up to newsletter There are around 10,000 chemicals defined as PFAS, and they are used in a huge range of products and processes, from cosmetics to industrial lubricants. But the health and environmental impacts of many of these chemicals are relatively understudied. One of the short-chain PFAS that is now particularly widespread across the world is trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) – which can form when pesticides, refrigerants and pharmaceuticals break down in the environment. The EA report confirmed that TFA is widespread in England, and a separate study published this week confirmed that it is also widespread across the UK more generally. “These findings add to the growing weight of evidence that PFAS pollution must be tackled at source if we are to protect our environment and our health,” says Hannah Evans , who worked on this second study and works with the UK environmental charity Fidra. “Other countries are already progressing towards this end… The UK cannot afford to fall further behind,” says Evans. Read more Wastewater treatment plants funnel PFAS into drinking water Currently, the EU is looking at a blanket ban on all PFAS chemicals, so that when specific chemicals are prohibited they aren’t simply replaced by another PFAS that may also eventually be identified as harmful and persistent in the environment. The UK government has said it is following this closely but has given no timescales on when a similar policy might be introduced. Alistair Boxall at the University of York, UK, says that the decline in legacy pollutants and increase in short-chain replacements was observed in a recently published European-wide monitoring study he took part in. He believes the change shows why bans that target the entire group of chemicals could offer a better way forward. “We seem to always be playing catch-up with chemicals like PFAS, so need to be much more agile in the way that we monitor and manage these substances. The idea of using grouping approaches could help,” says Boxall. Patrick Byrne at Liverpool John Moores University, UK, says that the grouping approach is useful and something that scientists have argued strongly for. Plant biology provides inspiration for PFAS replacement Forever chemicals are renowned for their durability and their non-stick properties, but they persist for years in the environment. An alternative inspired by plants doesn’t have the same problem He also says that the story isn’t over for PFOS and PFOA. Though they are decreasing globally, it’s important to remember they are still highly persistent and found in almost every water body. The levels of PFOS being recorded are still, in many cases, higher than the UK and EU Environmental Quality Standard, which is set to reflect the concentration above which the chemical will affect ecosystems. Currently, PFOS is the only individual PFAS with such a standard in England, but others are under development . “This report adds to our growing understanding of how PFAS enter our environment, but we must not wait for a complete picture before acting,” says Chloe Alexander , a campaigner at Wildlife and Countryside Link, an umbrella organisation in the UK that brings together many volunteer and charitable groups. “History is full of late lessons from early warnings, where ignored science allowed preventable harm to become widespread and, in some cases, irreversible,” says Alexander. “The longer it waits, the greater the risks to people and wildlife – and the higher the costs of clean-up and toxic waste disposal.”

item.title: CEO Jensen Huang's job is suddenly on the line at Nvidia
item.description: Nvidia’s board is set to decide the future of its founder Jensen Huang after revelations that he had a romantic relationship with a company executive, days after it emerged that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. The board held urgent talks on Wednesday night after news broke of the Nvidia chief executive’s relationship with Kimberly Powell, the chipmaker’s vice-president of healthcare, according to people familiar with the matter. The relationship with an Nvidia employee deepens an already damaging scandal for the $4.2 trillion semiconductor group. Huang on Sunday admitted to having an affair, two days after the FT reported his romantic links to an executive at an Nvidia client, who US officials believe is a Chinese intelligence asset. Read full article Comments

item.title: Olumide Oworu Declares House of Representatives Bid for Surulere Constituency 1 in 2027
item.description: Olumide Oworu has declared his candidacy for the Federal House of Representatives to represent Surulere Constituency 1 in 2027. Photo Credit: Olumide Oworu/Instagram Actor and media personality Olumide Oworu has declared his intention to contest for the Federal House of Representatives seat for Surulere Constituency 1 in the 2027 general elections. He will be running under the platform of the Allied Peoples Movement (APM). Olumide, who grew up in Surulere, Lagos, has a long-standing connection to the constituency. He began his acting career as a child, appearing in television productions such as Everyday People , before gaining wider recognition for his role in The Johnsons and other Nigerian film and television projects. This is his second attempt to enter legislative politics. In 2023, he declared his intention to contest for a seat in the Lagos State House of Assembly under the Labour Party. However, administrative challenges prevented his name from appearing on the final ballot. Olumide Oworu’s official campaign poster for the House of Representatives seat representing Surulere Constituency 1 under the Allied Peoples Movement. Photo Credit: Olumide Oworu/Instagram Reflecting on that experience in his candidacy announcement on Instagram, Olumide said the support he received from young people in Surulere had strengthened his belief in their readiness for more active participation in governance. “Despite the administrative hurdles that left our names off the final ballot, your resilience showed me that our vision was never a passing phase. Instead, it was the beginning of something much more significant,” he wrote. Explaining his decision to contest again, this time for a seat in the House of Representatives, he added: “We cannot afford to sit on the sidelines while our future is decided by a political class that won’t have to live with the consequences of today’s choices.” His campaign has highlighted issues including gaps in public services, community infrastructure and the participation of young Nigerians in policy decisions. Announcing his candidacy, he said he looked forward to continued support as he and his supporters worked towards what he described as a mission to “Reset Nigeria”. Olumide Oworu is contesting for a legislative seat in Surulere Constituency 1 under the APM platform. Photo Credit: Olumide Oworu/Instagram The post Olumide Oworu Declares House of Representatives Bid for Surulere Constituency 1 in 2027 appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: NASA kick-starts a fresh push to bring Mars samples home
item.description: null A long-term goal at NASA has been the ability to robotically haul back to Earth specimens from the Red Planet. NASA is kickstarting a new initiative for its troubled Mars Sample Return (MSR) program, called the Perseverance Sample Retrieval Architecture, or PSRA in space shorthand. The plan is to establish a fresh NASA strategy for gathering Mars samples collected by the Perseverance rover and launching them back to Earth. The PSRA initiative was noted on Nov. 9 by Tiffany Morgan, director of the NASA Mars Exploration Program (MEP), during the virtual meeting of the Mars Exploration Program Analysis Group (MEPAG). Here's the PSRA strategy: Develop impartial recommendations for retrieving the Martian samples collected by NASA's Perseverance Mars rover and deliver them to Earth Assess proposed mission requirements Review prior lessons learned Evaluate current capabilities and acquisition options Morgan noted that there will be a PSRA strategy team kickoff in January 2027 with a final report due in winter 2027-2028. Pick-me-ups The backdrop to the PSRA activity is that there's one busy rover already on the Red Planet snagging and bagging samples. NASA's Perseverance Mars rover remains on the prowl within Jezero Crater following its touchdown in February 2021. That car-sized robot has been grabbing select specimens from across the area and gingerly dropping the sealed pick-me-ups on the surface of Mars , as well as stuffing them inside the rover itself. Those collectibles may well hold signs of past life on the enigmatic, dusty and foreboding Red Planet. NASA and the European Space Agency have for years been intently plotting out plans to send future spacecraft to Mars and haul those Perseverance-plucked bits, pieces, and sniffs of atmosphere to Earth for rigorous inspection here on Earth using state-of-the-art equipment. This photomontage shows each of the sample tubes deposited by NASA's Perseverance Mars rover at the Three Forks sample depot, as viewed by the WATSON camera on the end of the rover's robotic arm. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS) Sticker shock However, over the years, multiple reviews of a NASA Mars Sample Return (MSR) project by independent groups have reported sticker shock findings. Indeed, one last price tag came in at about $11 billion, with samples being returned to Earth in 2040. That finding was deemed by NASA itself as too costly and not doable within an acceptable time frame. Yet another appraisal group ended up finding it feasible to return Mars samples as early as 2035 for a less costly ship and shoot cost of some $8 billion. How the PSRA review deals with MSR cost and a multitude of other concerns is in the to-be-determined column. Why samples now? In the first place, why are samples from Mars delivered by robotic means? item.dc:creator: Leonard David
item.content:encoded: null A long-term goal at NASA has been the ability to robotically haul back to Earth specimens from the Red Planet. NASA is kickstarting a new initiative for its troubled Mars Sample Return (MSR) program, called the Perseverance Sample Retrieval Architecture, or PSRA in space shorthand. The plan is to establish a fresh NASA strategy for gathering Mars samples collected by the Perseverance rover and launching them back to Earth. The PSRA initiative was noted on Nov. 9 by Tiffany Morgan, director of the NASA Mars Exploration Program (MEP), during the virtual meeting of the Mars Exploration Program Analysis Group (MEPAG). Here's the PSRA strategy: Develop impartial recommendations for retrieving the Martian samples collected by NASA's Perseverance Mars rover and deliver them to Earth Assess proposed mission requirements Review prior lessons learned Evaluate current capabilities and acquisition options Morgan noted that there will be a PSRA strategy team kickoff in January 2027 with a final report due in winter 2027-2028. Pick-me-ups The backdrop to the PSRA activity is that there's one busy rover already on the Red Planet snagging and bagging samples. NASA's Perseverance Mars rover remains on the prowl within Jezero Crater following its touchdown in February 2021. That car-sized robot has been grabbing select specimens from across the area and gingerly dropping the sealed pick-me-ups on the surface of Mars , as well as stuffing them inside the rover itself. Those collectibles may well hold signs of past life on the enigmatic, dusty and foreboding Red Planet. NASA and the European Space Agency have for years been intently plotting out plans to send future spacecraft to Mars and haul those Perseverance-plucked bits, pieces, and sniffs of atmosphere to Earth for rigorous inspection here on Earth using state-of-the-art equipment. This photomontage shows each of the sample tubes deposited by NASA's Perseverance Mars rover at the Three Forks sample depot, as viewed by the WATSON camera on the end of the rover's robotic arm. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS) Sticker shock However, over the years, multiple reviews of a NASA Mars Sample Return (MSR) project by independent groups have reported sticker shock findings. Indeed, one last price tag came in at about $11 billion, with samples being returned to Earth in 2040. That finding was deemed by NASA itself as too costly and not doable within an acceptable time frame. Yet another appraisal group ended up finding it feasible to return Mars samples as early as 2035 for a less costly ship and shoot cost of some $8 billion. How the PSRA review deals with MSR cost and a multitude of other concerns is in the to-be-determined column. Why samples now? In the first place, why are samples from Mars delivered by robotic means? Why not let a human expedition bring back the goods? Also speaking at MEPAG was Bruce Jakosky of the Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics at the University of Colorado Boulder and Department of Earth and Space Sciences at the University of Washington. Jakosky called for an integrated approach to planning human missions to Mars. He highlighted recommendations stemming from a workshop in which he participated, held last May and organized by Explore Mars, Inc. That report focused on the impact of MSR on reducing risk for human missions, rather than focusing on the science, Jakosky told Space.com. "The purpose is to understand the risk to astronauts and to hardware. The risk includes that from compounds that are present in the soil that are hazardous to astronauts if breathed in," said Jakosky. "This includes perchlorates and chloromethanes that have been identified already, and detection of other species that might be present. It also includes dust that can be breathed in by astronauts and that can affect hardware wear and tear," he said. During the MEPAG gathering, Jakosky flagged the importance of returning samples prior to human missions to Mars, such as: Identify and characterize known hazardous chemicals to ensure astronaut safety (e.g., perchlorates and chloromethanes), and look for possible additional hazardous chemicals Characterize very fine dust particles that could cause respiratory issues in astronauts Characterize dust and regolith properties for spacesuit design and wear patterns Search in advance of the arrival of humans for evidence of extant life that could interact with terrestrial life Enhance astronaut effectiveness on the surface and science return from human missions by providing initial context and analysis Demonstrate successful round-trip to Mars Demonstrate successful round-trip travel, including entry, descent, landing and ascent from the surface of Mars. Demonstrate implementation of planetary protection protocols. While human missions would not use the same approaches, what we learn from doing these would make the approach for humans much easier to plan and implement. China's program Diagram of China's proposed Tianwen 3 Mars sample return mission. (Image credit: The University of Hong Kong/Zengqian Hou, et al.) Yet one more forcing factor for NASA in yet another relook at MSR is that China is making progress on its Tianwen-3 Mars Sample Return mission. According to the China National Space Administration, the country's Tianwen-3 probe will have a lander, an ascender, a service capsule, an orbiter, and an Earth reentry module. Tianwen-3 appears on track getting the trek underway around 2028 on two Long March-5 heavy-lift carrier rockets from the Wenchang Space Launch Site in China's southernmost island province of Hainan. China's Tianwen-3 mission is dedicated to bring back to Earth roughly 500 grams of Red Planet collectibles in 2031.

item.description: USSF cites state department advisory about Qatar Competition set to kick off in eight days The US men’s national team have pulled out of the Fifa U-17 World Cup, which is due to kick off in Qatar in just over a week. In a letter sent to players explaining the decision, the US Soccer Federation cited safety concerns for players and staff, referring them to the US state department’s travel advisory for Qatar, which encourages citizens to reconsider travel to the country “due to risk of armed conflict” and asks government employees to obtain special authorization to do so. “Unfortunately, in light of current circumstances … we are no longer able to participate in the tournament,” US Soccer’s letter to players reads. “The wellbeing of our players and staff will always be our top priority. item.title: We can't see Fast Radio Bursts but we can now hear them thanks to a Finnish Cathedral
item.description:
Sharmila Kuthunur is an independent space journalist based in Bengaluru, India. Her work has also appeared in Scientific American, Science, Astronomy and Live Science, among other publications. She holds a master's degree in journalism from Northeastern University in Boston. 

Fast radio bursts, flashes of energy from faraway galaxies, are invisible to our eyes. However, we can now hear their melody, thanks to a composer who has turned them into sound. Fast radio bursts, or FRBs , are among the most extreme events in the universe, releasing as much energy in a millisecond as the sun puts out in three days and briefly outshining entire galaxies. Since the first FRB was discovered in 2007, astronomers have detected thousands of them; however, exactly how these cosmic flares are launched remains poorly understood. Recent evidence points to at least one burst coming from the environment around a rotating neutron star. Despite their power, FRBs last only a few thousandths of a second before vanishing into space. Catching one takes luck, as a telescope has to be pointed at the right patch of sky at the right moment. That changed with CHIME (the Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment) in British Columbia. With a very wide field of view and a supercomputer to process its data, CHIME more than quadrupled the number of known FRBs in its first year of operation alone. Between 2018 and 2023, CHIME recorded 4,539 bursts from 3,641 sources. As pulses of radio waves, our eyes haven't evolved to see FRBs, nor can we hear them as they aren't sound waves. Well, not until now. "Artist and composer Andrew Melchior turned all of the CHIME bursts into sound for "The Logos," an installation that has played daily at Oulu Cathedral in Finland since early April and is scheduled to run through the end of the year. Melchior and Kiyoshi Masui, an associate professor of physics at MIT, "sonified" the bursts, translating data into acoustics so that human ears can hear them. The structure of each real signal is mapped to varying musical pitches and played through 12 loudspeakers spread throughout the cathedral. The result is a range of tones, with distant FRBs humming, rumbling, popping, and whistling. The signals are old by any human measure. According to a description on Melchior's website , the youngest in the work are about 50 million years old, and the oldest are about 8 to 9 billion years old. An animation shows the random appearance of fast radio bursts (FRBs) across the sky (Image credit: NRAO Outreach/T. Jarrett (IPAC/Caltech); B. Saxton, NRAO/AUI/NSF)) Physics also plays a role in what is heard. Each burst arrives with its high frequencies first and sweeps downward, stretched by its journey through intergalactic gas, "and you can hear that dispersion as it falls from the dome," Melchior told Space.com by email. That changed with CHIME (the Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment) in British Columbia. With a very wide field of view and a supercomputer to process its data, CHIME more than quadrupled the number of known FRBs in its first year of operation alone. Between 2018 and 2023, CHIME recorded 4,539 bursts from 3,641 sources. As pulses of radio waves, our eyes haven't evolved to see FRBs, nor can we hear them as they aren't sound waves. Well, not until now. "Artist and composer Andrew Melchior turned all of the CHIME bursts into sound for "The Logos," an installation that has played daily at Oulu Cathedral in Finland since early April and is scheduled to run through the end of the year. Melchior and Kiyoshi Masui, an associate professor of physics at MIT, "sonified" the bursts, translating data into acoustics so that human ears can hear them. The structure of each real signal is mapped to varying musical pitches and played through 12 loudspeakers spread throughout the cathedral. The result is a range of tones, with distant FRBs humming, rumbling, popping, and whistling. The signals are old by any human measure. According to a description on Melchior's website , the youngest in the work are about 50 million years old, and the oldest are about 8 to 9 billion years old. An animation shows the random appearance of fast radio bursts (FRBs) across the sky (Image credit: NRAO Outreach/T. Jarrett (IPAC/Caltech); B. Saxton, NRAO/AUI/NSF)) Physics also plays a role in what is heard. Each burst arrives with its high frequencies first and sweeps downward, stretched by its journey through intergalactic gas, "and you can hear that dispersion as it falls from the dome," Melchior told Space.com by email. Since their discovery in 2007, the bursts are also still yielding discoveries. Last month, astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope pinpointed the host galaxy of the most distant FRB yet, one that went off when the universe was only about 3 billion years old. The galaxy, a small, young, star-forming dwarf, was far smaller than expected. That makes it harder to square with the theory that FRBs come from merging neutron stars, researchers say, which would take billions of years to occur. This fits better with a second theory, in which a young, highly magnetic neutron star called a magnetar produces the burst soon after a massive star explodes, according to NASA . An illustration of a magnetar launching a FRB (Image credit: Robert Lea (created with Canva)) Back on Earth, an upcoming event at Oulu Cathedral offers a more immediate encounter with the bursts. On Nov. 21, 30 singers will stand among the audience and "sing back to the sky in Finnish" while Melchior plays the bursts live from a keyboard, he told Space.com by email. "The fast flashes will echo as snare-like beats bouncing through the cathedral," Masui said in a previous MIT statement . "It should feel rich and layered, while also revealing something real about how these signals travel across billions of years of cosmic space before reaching Earth."
