item.title: On this day in space! Nov. 11, 1966: NASA launches Gemini 12 mission with astronaut icons Buzz Aldrin and Jim Lovell aboard
item.description: null On Nov. 11, 1966, the Gemini 12 mission launched an astronaut crew into orbit and set the stage for NASA's Apollo program to land humans on the moon. Gemini 12 was the last mission of the Gemini program. It had two astronauts on board: Jim Lovell and Buzz Aldrin . NASA wanted to send humans to the moon. But first, it needed to make sure crews had the right skills, like docking vehicles in space and taking spacewalks. Before Gemini 12, astronauts struggled with spacewalks because there weren't enough handholds on their spacecraft. NASA made some spacewalk changes for Gemini 12. Aldrin performed three spacewalks and spent more than five hours working in space with no major problems. Gemini 12 also successfully docked to an unpiloted Agena booster that launched the same day. The astronauts returned to Earth after four days in space. Both Aldrin and Lovell went on to join the Apollo program . Aldrin became the second person to walk on the moon during Apollo 11 , and Lovell became the commander of Apollo 13 . The Gemini 12 astronauts James Lovell and Edwin Aldrin lifted off aboard a Titan launch vehicle from the Kennedy Space Center on November 11, 1966, an hour and a half after their Agena target vehicle was orbited by an Atlas rocket. (Image credit: NASA/MSFC) Why it mattered Gemini 12 may have closed out NASA's Gemini program of two-person space missions, but it established the mission also established the fundamentals of spacewalking that Apollo astronauts would use when they walked on the moon. It's fitting that Aldrin was the primary spacewalker of the mission. A rookie astronaut (and the first to earn a Ph.D.), Aldrin set a precedent by training for his spacewalk in a neutral buoyancy pool in Maryland to better simulate working in weightlessness. Then he did it again as the second person to walk on the moon on Apollo 11. "This approach became so successful, underwater training has become the primary spacewalk training method used by the United State, Russia and China," NASA officials said in a mission overview . "Today, NASA’s Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory in Houston is large enough to include mockups of major sections of the International Space Station . As such, it is the largest indoor body of water in the world, with 6.2 million gallons of water." item.content:encoded: null On Nov. 11, 1966, the Gemini 12 mission launched an astronaut crew into orbit and set the stage for NASA's Apollo program to land humans on the moon. The astronauts returned to Earth after four days in space. Both Aldrin and Lovell went on to join the Apollo program . Aldrin became the second person to walk on the moon during Apollo 11 , and Lovell became the commander of Apollo 13 . The Gemini 12 astronauts James Lovell and Edwin Aldrin lifted off aboard a Titan launch vehicle from the Kennedy Space Center on November 11, 1966, an hour and a half after their Agena target vehicle was orbited by an Atlas rocket. (Image credit: NASA/MSFC) Why it mattered Gemini 12 may have closed out NASA's Gemini program of two-person space missions, but it established the mission also established the fundamentals of spacewalking that Apollo astronauts would use when they walked on the moon. It's fitting that Aldrin was the primary spacewalker of the mission. A rookie astronaut (and the first to earn a Ph.D.), Aldrin set a precedent by training for his spacewalk in a neutral buoyancy pool in Maryland to better simulate working in weightlessness. Then he did it again as the second person to walk on the moon on Apollo 11. "This approach became so successful, underwater training has become the primary spacewalk training method used by the United State, Russia and China," NASA officials said in a mission overview . "Today, NASA’s Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory in Houston is large enough to include mockups of major sections of the International Space Station . As such, it is the largest indoor body of water in the world, with 6.2 million gallons of water." Astronaut Buzz Aldrin practices spacewalking tasks for Gemini 12 in an underwater mockup of his spacecraft in 1966. NASA The Gemini 12 astronauts walk out to their launch pad with signs on their back denoting "THE END" of the Gemini program. NASA/MSFC NASA The Agena docking target for Gemini 12 launched into orbit just over 90 minutes ahead of Lovell (the mission commander) and Aldrin. Aldrin ended up using a sextant to help Lovell rendevous with the agena after they lost radar lock within 74 miles of the vehicle. During his spacewalks, Aldrin installed handrails, used foot restraints and other tools that have since become routine on spacewalks in orbit. They also tested tools and techniques that Aldrin and other moonwalks would use on the moon . Gemini 12 also tested a computer-controlled reentry technique when it returned to Earth on Nov. 15, landing Lovell and Aldrin just 3 miles from their target near their recovery ship the USS Wasp in the Atlantic Ocean, about 600 miles east of Cape Canaveral. item.title: Seven New Tracks From Rema? E-Mortal Boy (EMB) Is Coming Next Week
item.description: Rema announces his upcoming 7-track EP, E-Mortal Boy (EMB), scheduled for release on 20 November 2026. Photo Credit: Rema/Instagram Rema is getting ready to give fans a fresh body of music! The Nigerian singer has officially announced that his new seven-track EP, E-Mortal Boy ( EMB ), will be released next Friday, 20 November 2026. It’s been a little while since his last EP, so there’s plenty of reason for fans to be curious about what he has been working on. The 26-year-old Benin City star first introduced himself to listeners with his self-titled debut EP in 2019, released under Mavin Records and Jonzing World. Since then, he’s built an impressive catalogue, moving between different sounds while taking his music to audiences around the world. His 2022 debut album, Rave & Roses, marked a major turning point in his career, followed by the return to a more raw Afrobeats sound on the 2023 EP Ravage. In 2024, he switched things up again with HEIS , his high-intensity sophomore album, which earned him further international attention. Rema preparing for the release of his new EP E-Mortal Boy following his singles TEA and Oh No. Photo Credit: Rema/Instagram Now, Rema is opening another chapter with E-Mortal Boy (EMB). The project already has two singles to introduce its sound: “ Oh No ” and the fan-favourite “ TEA “. Both tracks give listeners an early taste of the music surrounding the new release, although Rema is keeping the rest of the project under wraps for now. The full tracklist and details of any featured artists have yet to be revealed. With seven tracks, E-Mortal Boy (EMB) will be Rema’s first EP since Ravage and his latest project following HEIS . The singer is set to release it on digital streaming platforms on 20 November, giving fans a new collection to get into as he continues to build on an already eventful musical journey. The post Seven New Tracks From Rema? E-Mortal Boy (EMB) Is Coming Next Week appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: T-Mobile illegally imposed 50GB cap on low-income home Internet plan, NY says
item.description: T-Mobile violated a New York state law by imposing a 50GB-per-month data cap and reducing speeds to less than a megabit per second on home Internet plans it is required to offer people with low incomes, New York government officials alleged. T-Mobile agreed to a settlement requiring it to scrap the data and speed limits, to offer the required low-income plans to more parts of the state, and to make it easier for customers to find information about the plans. The settlement requires T-Mobile to eliminate the speed limits and expand availability of the plans within 120 days. The alleged legal violation and the settlement are related to T-Mobile's wireless home Internet service, not the company's mobile plans. Governor Kathy Hochul and New York Attorney General Letitia James announced the settlement on Monday, saying that a state investigation found T-Mobile violated the New York Affordable Broadband Act (ABA). Read full article Comments

item.title: Anduril says its first satellite can see adversaries maneuver in orbital night
item.description: Anduril Industries has announced the successful demonstration of a new satellite-based sensor designed to track other spacecraft that may be hiding their maneuvers in Earth's shadow. Funded with Anduril's internal capital, the company's oven-sized satellite launched on a SpaceX rideshare mission in July with a package of tech demo payloads: an edge-compute processor, a power-management system adaptable to different mission types, and a long-wave infrared space sensor capable of detecting other objects in orbit. Anduril reported on the success of the tech demo mission Tuesday. The company's satellite, named Anduril-216, flies about 590 km (366 mi) above Earth, spending about one-third of each orbit in darkness. Anduril-216's night passes allow its infrared imager to shine. Read full article Comments

item.title: Awar Odhiang Named Model of the Year at The Fashion Awards 2026
item.description: Awar Odhiang featured in Vogue wearing a floral printed dress and sculpted oversized rose headpiece. Photo Credit: Awar Odhiang/Instagram Remember the model who turned the finale of Matthieu Blazy ‘s first Chanel show into one of the most talked-about runway moments of 2025? That was Awar Odhiang, and she has another major reason to celebrate. The South Sudanese-Canadian model has been named Model of the Year at The Fashion Awards 2026. The 25-year-old will receive the honour at London’s Royal Albert Hall on 30 November. Born in a refugee camp in Ethiopia and raised in Canada, Awar’s journey to the international fashion scene has taken her from being discovered in Alberta to walking some of the world’s biggest runways. She is now represented by major modelling agencies across London, Milan, Paris and New York. Awar Odhiang walking the red carpet at the 2026 Met Gala in New York City. Photo Credit: Awar Odhiang/Instagram Her runway résumé includes shows for Prada, Versace, Miu Miu, Saint Laurent and Jacquemus, but it was her appearance at Chanel’s Spring/Summer 2026 show in October 2025 that introduced her to an even wider audience. Closing Matthieu Blazy’s first collection for the fashion house, Awar wore the show’s bridal look, featuring an oversized white shirt and a voluminous, colourful feathered skirt. But it was what happened at the finale that captured everyone’s attention. As the models gathered for their final walk, Awar broke formation, smiling, clapping and twirling in her skirt. When Blazy appeared, she ran towards him and embraced him. The spontaneous moment quickly went viral, with fashion fans celebrating the joy she brought to the runway. It was also a historic appearance: Awar became only the third Black woman to close a Chanel show in the house’s 115-year history, after Alek Wek and Adut Akech. Model of the Year 2026 winner Awar Odhiang backstage at the Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show. Photo Credit: Awar Odhiang/Instagram Since then, her career has continued to gather pace. Awar has appeared on eight international magazine covers this year and fronted campaigns for Chanel, Chloé, Louis Vuitton, Saint Laurent, Loro Piana and H&M. She has also used her growing platform to speak up for greater representation and inclusion of Black models in the luxury fashion industry. Awar Odhiang in Daniel Roseberry’s Schiaparelli Spring 2026 Haute Couture collection in Paris. Photo Credit: Awar Odhiang/Instagram Her Model of the Year recognition celebrates a remarkable year of runway, editorial and campaign work, as well as the influence she continues to have beyond the catwalk. On 30 November, she’ll take that recognition to the Royal Albert Hall, adding another milestone to a career that is still unfolding. Awar Odhiang wearing a tailored blazer during international fashion week. Photo Credit: Awar Odhiang/Instagram Awar Odhiang attending the 2026 Met Gala in custom Chanel by Matthieu Blazy. Photo Credit: Awar Odhiang/Instagram The post Awar Od

item.title: NASA's secret weapon in the lunar space race may be ... procurement reform?
item.description: Senior NASA officials held a lengthy news conference last weekend, laying out a series of lunar contract awards, new contract opportunities, and mission decisions. They followed one after the other: landers, nuclear-powered rovers, scouting drones, power generation, storage, and communication satellites. It never seemed to end. "Hopefully, we're keeping industry on their toes trying to catch up to all the solicitations we're doing," said Carlos García-Galán, manager of the Moon Base Program, more than 90 minutes into the news conference. item.title: Complaint filed to IRS in relation to Fifa head Gianni Infantino’s housekeeper
item.description: It calls for inquiry into claims she was on Fifa payroll Fifa: Infantino personally pays for ‘any domestic staff’ A complaint has been filed to the United States Internal Revenue Service calling for an investigation into claims an individual on the Fifa payroll was working privately as a housekeeper for Gianni Infantino. If the IRS investigates and finds the claims to be proven then Fifa could lose its tax-exempt status in the US. Fifa has 501(c)(4) status in the country, a category for organisations “created to promote community welfare for charitable, educational or recreational purposes”. Continue reading...

item.title: Thomas Tuchel keeps laser focus on ‘unfinished business’ with England
item.description: Head coach did not insert release clause into contract Tuchel ‘open to everything’ including staying after Euros Thomas Tuchel will not be going anywhere before Euro 2028. Mauricio Pochettino is expected to leave his role as the USA men’s head coach to replace Michael Carrick at Manchester United , but Tuchel has not lost his passion for international football and has revealed he did not insert a release clause when he extended his deal as England’s manager this year. It will not matter whether there is an approach from a big club before the next tournament. United can pay about £7m to get Pochettino out of his deal, but the Football Association does not have to worry about being forced to let Tuchel go. “There’s no intention [of leaving],” Tuchel said. “I signed the contract. I want to stay until the Euros. I want to do the Euros. We have unfinished business.” Continue reading...

item.title: Blood-thinning drug limits cartilage damage and relieves osteoarthritis pain
item.description: Coloured X-ray of osteoarthritis of the knee ALAIN POL/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY A drug that prevents blood clots reduced pain and improved mobility in mice and monkeys with knee osteoarthritis. The approach seems to partly work by reducing inflammatory signals that degrade cartilage. Osteoarthritis is caused by the wear and tear of cartilage that cushions the ends of bones, leading to inflammation, pain and stiffness. It affects more than 500 million people worldwide. Painkillers and anti-inflammatory drugs can relieve symptoms, but no approved drugs halt or slow worsening of the disease. “We have nothing to offer our patients apart from suggesting weight loss, or offering drugs that provide pain relief,” says Tonia Vincent at the University of Oxford, who wasn’t involved in the study. Advertisement Read more The best non-drug therapies to relieve the pain of knee osteoarthritis It is widely thought that inflammatory molecules called TNF-alpha and IL-1-beta drive inflammation that worsens osteoarthritis. This has led to clinical trials testing drugs that target either of these molecules. But these have been unsuccessful, potentially because these molecules compensate for each other when one is blocked, according to Chuan-Ju Liu at Yale University and his colleagues. To explore whether targeting both molecules may be more effective, the researchers surgically removed part of the cartilage in the left knee joints of eight monkeys to mimic wear and tear that triggers osteoarthritis. A month later, four of the monkeys took a daily dose of a drug called dabigatran, mixed into their food. Dabigatran is commonly used to prevent blood clots in people at increased risk of strokes, but has also been shown to block inflammatory signals via both TNF-alpha and IL-1-beta. The remaining monkeys ate their usual food as a control. Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter After seven months, MRI scans revealed that the left-knee cartilage in monkeys on dabigratan was about 60 per cent thicker, on average, compared to the control monkeys. This suggests that the drug reduced cartilage damage, slowing the progression of osteoarthritis, says Liu. Monkeys on dabigratan also had a roughly 15 per cent greater range of motion in their left knee than the control monkeys. “Monkeys receiving dabigatran showed a more natural walking pattern and a greater range of knee movement,” says Liu. “These improvements are consistent with reduced joint stiffness and discomfort.” In further experiments, the team confirmed their findings in mice with surgically-induced knee osteoarthritis, which also revealed that dabigratan reduced inflammation in the knee by about 60 per cent. item.dc:creator: Carissa Wong
item.content:encoded: Coloured X-ray of osteoarthritis of the knee ALAIN POL/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY A drug that prevents blood clots reduced pain and improved mobility in mice and monkeys with knee osteoarthritis. The approach seems to partly work by reducing inflammatory signals that degrade cartilage. Osteoarthritis is caused by the wear and tear of cartilage that cushions the ends of bones, leading to inflammation, pain and stiffness. It affects more than 500 million people worldwide. Painkillers and anti-inflammatory drugs can relieve symptoms, but no approved drugs halt or slow worsening of the disease. “We have nothing to offer our patients apart from suggesting weight loss, or offering drugs that provide pain relief,” says Tonia Vincent at the University of Oxford, who wasn’t involved in the study. Advertisement Read more The best non-drug therapies to relieve the pain of knee osteoarthritis It is widely thought that inflammatory molecules called TNF-alpha and IL-1-beta drive inflammation that worsens osteoarthritis. This has led to clinical trials testing drugs that target either of these molecules. But these have been unsuccessful, potentially because these molecules compensate for each other when one is blocked, according to Chuan-Ju Liu at Yale University and his colleagues. To explore whether targeting both molecules may be more effective, the researchers surgically removed part of the cartilage in the left knee joints of eight monkeys to mimic wear and tear that triggers osteoarthritis. A month later, four of the monkeys took a daily dose of a drug called dabigatran, mixed into their food. Dabigatran is commonly used to prevent blood clots in people at increased risk of strokes, but has also been shown to block inflammatory signals via both TNF-alpha and IL-1-beta. The remaining monkeys ate their usual food as a control. Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter After seven months, MRI scans revealed that the left-knee cartilage in monkeys on dabigratan was about 60 per cent thicker, on average, compared to the control monkeys. This suggests that the drug reduced cartilage damage, slowing the progression of osteoarthritis, says Liu. Monkeys on dabigratan also had a roughly 15 per cent greater range of motion in their left knee than the control monkeys. “Monkeys receiving dabigatran showed a more natural walking pattern and a greater range of knee movement,” says Liu. “These improvements are consistent with reduced joint stiffness and discomfort.” In further experiments, the team confirmed their findings in mice with surgically-induced knee osteoarthritis, which also revealed that dabigratan reduced inflammation in the knee by about 60 per cent. Injections of drug-filled nanoparticles may relieve arthritis pain A drug called pazopanib is known to provide brief relief from arthritis pain – encapsulating it in nanoparticles can make its effects last much longer, research in mice suggests The findings suggest dabigratan could slow the progression of osteoarthritis in people. “They’ve used the best [animal] models we have of osteoarthritis,” says Vincent. “If the findings can be replicated by another research group, you would certainly consider trying a small clinical trial,” she says. But it is unclear whether the approach can reverse damage that has already occurred, says Liu. Another limitation is that giving people a drug that reduces blood clotting puts them at greater risk of bleeds, so the researchers are now developing drugs that target TNF-alpha and IL-1-beta without reducing clotting, which they will test in mice before any clinical trials, says Liu. However, Vincent says prior studies suggest that inhibiting molecules involved in blood clotting may relieve osteoarthritis symptoms, which might mean that some of dabigratan’s benefits are due to its anti-clotting, rather than anti-inflammatory, effect. Further research that compares dabigatran with drugs that target TNF-alpha and IL-1-beta without the clotting effects should help to clarify this, she says. Journal Reference: Science Translational Medicine DOI: 10.1126/scitranslmed.aec8494

item.title: Andy Weir's 'Exoplanet' just landed on Audible, but what actually makes an exoplanet habitable?
item.description: null Imagine you’ve crash-landed on an alien planet. Your ship is destroyed, your oxygen supply is dangerously low, and the landscape around you is completely unknown. Where would you begin looking for clues to your survival? Surprisingly, the best place to start could be the star overhead. This is the predicament that three crew members of the Wild Blue Yonder face in Audible’s new sci-fi thriller, "Exoplanet." This sci-fi thriller is written by acclaimed comic writer Benjamin Percy, executive produced by Andy Weir (Project Hail Mary, The Martian), and features an all-star voice cast including Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose, and John Leguizamo . Stranded on an unfamiliar planet, they encounter volcanic wastelands, unknown skies, and environments that seem to defy reason. But behind the extraordinary events of this audio drama is a very real scientific question: what makes a planet habitable? Learning from the stars An artist's concept illustrates a young, red dwarf star surrounded by three planets. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) In “Exoplanet”, the crew view skies that are not only unfamiliar but also seemingly different from one another. One character sees a sun as so dim that he can look directly at it, while another suffers under a blazing heat, surrounded by stretches of sun-scorched red rock. For astronomers, the light emitted by a star is one of the most crucial tools for understanding planets orbiting it. Using a technique called spectroscopy , astronomers split starlight into its constituent wavelengths, producing a spectrum much like a rainbow. By studying this spectrum, they can investigate the temperature, composition, and other physical properties of the star. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) However, stellar temperature is only part of the picture. The amount of energy a planet receives depends on both the luminosity of the star and its orbital distance. Astronomers use these measurements to determine whether a world lies in the habitable zone of a star, where temperatures could allow liquid water to exist on the surface given a suitable atmosphere. A planet orbiting a cool red dwarf would need to be much closer to its star than Earth is to the Sun to be in this habitable zone. Unfortunately, being in this zone is no guarantee of a planetary paradise. Hostile stars Black holes are bad news for life, but living stars provide just as many problems. (Image credit: Audible) A planet that sits comfortably in the habitable zone is ultimately still at the mercy of its star. Stars emit more than just the light we see. Ultraviolet radiation and X-rays can interact with planetary atmospheres, altering chemistry and even contributing to the loss of the atmosphere . Violent stellar flares can produce bursts of high-energy radiation. A planet could offer a wonderfully balmy temperature, only to be bombarded with radiation from the host star. The age of a star matters too. Young stars tend to be more active, with radiation that could erode a pla
item.dc:creator: Alix Freckelton
item.content:encoded: null Imagine you’ve crash-landed on an alien planet. Your ship is destroyed, your oxygen supply is dangerously low, and the landscape around you is completely unknown. Where would you begin looking for clues to your survival? Surprisingly, the best place to start could be the star overhead. This is the predicament that three crew members of the Wild Blue Yonder face in Audible’s new sci-fi thriller, "Exoplanet." This sci-fi thriller is written by acclaimed comic writer Benjamin Percy, executive produced by Andy Weir (Project Hail Mary, The Martian), and features an all-star voice cast including Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose, and John Leguizamo . Stranded on an unfamiliar planet, they encounter volcanic wastelands, unknown skies, and environments that seem to defy reason. But behind the extraordinary events of this audio drama is a very real scientific question: what makes a planet habitable? Learning from the stars An artist's concept illustrates a young, red dwarf star surrounded by three planets. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) In “Exoplanet”, the crew view skies that are not only unfamiliar but also seemingly different from one another. One character sees a sun as so dim that he can look directly at it, while another suffers under a blazing heat, surrounded by stretches of sun-scorched red rock. For astronomers, the light emitted by a star is one of the most crucial tools for understanding planets orbiting it. Using a technique called spectroscopy , astronomers split starlight into its constituent wavelengths, producing a spectrum much like a rainbow. By studying this spectrum, they can investigate the temperature, composition, and other physical properties of the star. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) However, stellar temperature is only part of the picture. The amount of energy a planet receives depends on both the luminosity of the star and its orbital distance. Astronomers use these measurements to determine whether a world lies in the habitable zone of a star, where temperatures could allow liquid water to exist on the surface given a suitable atmosphere. A planet orbiting a cool red dwarf would need to be much closer to its star than Earth is to the Sun to be in this habitable zone. Unfortunately, being in this zone is no guarantee of a planetary paradise. Hostile stars Black holes are bad news for life, but living stars provide just as many problems. (Image credit: Audible) A planet that sits comfortably in the habitable zone is ultimately still at the mercy of its star. Stars emit more than just the light we see. Ultraviolet radiation and X-rays can interact with planetary atmospheres, altering chemistry and even contributing to the loss of the atmosphere . Violent stellar flares can produce bursts of high-energy radiation. A planet could offer a wonderfully balmy temperature, only to be bombarded with radiation from the host star. The age of a star matters too. Young stars tend to be more active, with radiation that could erode a planet’s atmosphere over time. Meanwhile, as stars age and evolve, their changing luminosities can drastically alter the conditions a planet experiences. For the stranded crew in “Exoplanet”, understanding the star overhead may therefore be as important as knowing the landscape beneath their feet. Is the air breathable? NASA illustration of Kepler-186f, the first Earth-size planet to be discovered in a habitable zone. (Image credit: NASA Ames/SETI Institute/JPL-CalTech via Wikimedia Commons) Even if a planet has survived all the complications we’ve just thrown at it, there’s still a rather important question: could we actually breathe the air? In "Exoplanet", one crew member discovers that the planet’s atmosphere contains enough oxygen for him to breathe without his spacesuit. On Earth, oxygen makes up around 21% of our atmosphere. However, finding a similar percentage on another planet wouldn’t automatically mean the air is safe to breathe. Atmospheric pressure matters just as much . At high altitudes on Earth, the oxygen percentage remains the same, but the lower pressure means less oxygen is available to our lungs. Oxygen isn’t the only concern, either. The fictional planet’s volcanic landscape releases gases such as sulfur dioxide and hydrogen sulfide, both of which are hazardous at high concentrations. Even an oxygen-rich atmosphere could still be lethal. Searching for life An artist illustration of exoplanet K2-18b, an exoplanet orbiting a red dwarf. (Image credit: Hubble, M. Kornmesser via Wikimedia commons) But what if you don't just need to know if a planet is habitable? What if you need to know if something already lives there? Before the Wild Blue Yonder arrived at the planet, probes detected dimethyl sulfide, a molecule we associate with biological activity on Earth . This is a beautifully timely detail, as this very molecule has been at the heart of a scientific debate about one of the most intriguing exoplanets discovered so far. Astronomers have investigated possible signs of dimethyl sulfide in the atmosphere of K2-18 b , an exoplanet orbiting a red dwarf. However, both the detection itself and the biological interpretation remain heavily disputed . Astronomers can study the starlight that filters through exoplanet atmospheres, searching for signatures of molecules that may be signs of life. (Image credit: NASA, ESA and A. Feild (STScI)) The challenge is that detecting a single molecule isn’t definitive evidence of life. Its presence can be influenced by factors other than biology, like atmospheric chemistry and stellar radiation. Understanding whether such a molecule could actually indicate life means studying not just the planet’s atmosphere, but also the radiation it receives from its star. More than Earth Mark 2 (Image credit: Audible) Astronomers have discovered thousands of exoplanets. Understanding whether any could support life is, however, an extraordinary challenge. The distance between the planet and the star might give us a good clue, but its atmosphere, geology, and stellar environment are all interconnected in determining whether life could survive. For the unfortunate crew of the Wild Blue Yonder, those distinctions could mean the difference between survival and utter disaster. We might one day identify a planet with Earth-like temperatures, liquid water, and abundant oxygen. But even then, there’s still a huge gap dividing a potentially habitable planet from one where we could safely remove our helmets. "Exoplanet" is available now exclusively from Audible. It is free for members of its subscription tiers or available to purchase separately. One crew. One planet. Three timelines. No one survives alone. A sci-fi thriller executive produced by Andy Weir (#1 bestselling author of Project Hail Mary , The Martian ), with an all-star cast led by Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose and John Leguizamo. Exoplanet is free for Audible members, but also available for purchase separately. View Deal

item.title: The Francophone African Music Industries Fair (SIMA) announces its 3rd Edition in Republic of Benin | November 12th – 13th
item.description: The Francophone African Music Industries Fair (SIMA) announces the third edition of the event, taking place on November 12–13, 2026, in Cotonou, Republic of Benin. Following its previous edition, which brought together more than 6,700 participants and over 3,000 industry professionals, this pan-African gathering dedicated to the cultural and creative industries returns with a clear ambition: African Music: From the Stage to Global Influence. SIMA 2026 is supported by major institutional and private-sector partners, including the Ministry of Culture, Arts and Heritage of Benin,the Ministry of Tourism and Foreign Trade of Benin,the Embassy of France in Côte d’Ivoire,the BOAD Foundation, as well as SACEM, Sony Music and Warner Music Africa. These partnerships reflect the growing interest in the development and structuring of Africa’s cultural and creative industries. For the second consecutive year, Benin will host SIMA, in line with the country’s broader efforts to strengthen the role of the cultural and creative industries in the structural transformation of its economy and to enhance its cultural influence at both regional and international levels. Co-founded in 2022 by cultural entrepreneur Mamby Diomandé and artist and producer Pit Baccardi , SIMA has established itself as a platform dedicated to structuring, connecting and developing Africa’s creative ecosystems. By placing music at the heart of a broader reflection on the transformation of culture and the creative industries, SIMA also seeks to address the technological shifts reshaping the sector—from artificial intelligence to new ways of creating, distributing and consuming content. At a time when Africa’s creative economy could generate up to 20 million jobs by 2030, the 2026 edition aims to take a further step forward by contributing to the positioning of African creativity as a powerful driver of soft power, value creation and international influence. “African music is no longer simply a cultural phenomenon: it has become a force of influence. Our challenge now is to transform this influence into sustainable economic power. SIMA aims to build connections between creators, investors, institutions and markets so that the international visibility of our talents translates into measurable data, content monetization, economic opportunities, jobs and value creation for the continent.” Mamby Diomandé , Co-Founder of SIMA Three Priorities for Turning Creativity into Economic Power To address the challenges of a rapidly evolving global market, SIMA 2026 will structure its programme around three key priorities. The first focuses on competitiveness and internationalization, with the aim of strengthening the economic performance of industry stakeholders and facilitating the international export of African talent. item.content:encoded: The Francophone African Music Industries Fair (SIMA) announces the third edition of the event, taking place on November 12–13, 2026, in Cotonou, Republic of Benin. Following its previous edition, which brought together more than 6,700 participants and over 3,000 industry professionals, this pan-African gathering dedicated to the cultural and creative industries returns with a clear ambition: African Music: From the Stage to Global Influence. SIMA 2026 is supported by major institutional and private-sector partners, including the Ministry of Culture, Arts and Heritage of Benin,the Ministry of Tourism and Foreign Trade of Benin,the Embassy of France in Côte d’Ivoire,the BOAD Foundation, as well as SACEM, Sony Music and Warner Music Africa. These partnerships reflect the growing interest in the development and structuring of Africa’s cultural and creative industries. For the second consecutive year, Benin will host SIMA, in line with the country’s broader efforts to strengthen the role of the cultural and creative industries in the structural transformation of its economy and to enhance its cultural influence at both regional and international levels. Co-founded in 2022 by cultural entrepreneur Mamby Diomandé and artist and producer Pit Baccardi , SIMA has established itself as a platform dedicated to structuring, connecting and developing Africa’s creative ecosystems. By placing music at the heart of a broader reflection on the transformation of culture and the creative industries, SIMA also seeks to address the technological shifts reshaping the sector—from artificial intelligence to new ways of creating, distributing and consuming content. At a time when Africa’s creative economy could generate up to 20 million jobs by 2030, the 2026 edition aims to take a further step forward by contributing to the positioning of African creativity as a powerful driver of soft power, value creation and international influence. “African music is no longer simply a cultural phenomenon: it has become a force of influence. Our challenge now is to transform this influence into sustainable economic power. SIMA aims to build connections between creators, investors, institutions and markets so that the international visibility of our talents translates into measurable data, content monetization, economic opportunities, jobs and value creation for the continent.” Mamby Diomandé , Co-Founder of SIMA Three Priorities for Turning Creativity into Economic Power To address the challenges of a rapidly evolving global market, SIMA 2026 will structure its programme around three key priorities. The first focuses on competitiveness and internationalization, with the aim of strengthening the economic performance of industry stakeholders and facilitating the international export of African talent. The second emphasizes cross-sector collaboration, bringing music closer to fashion, film, tourism, sports and other creative industries in order to unlock new revenue opportunities. The third focuses on public policy, intellectual property and regulatory frameworks, with the ambition of developing concrete recommendations and strengthening the mechanisms that will enable the sector to better capture the value it generates. Beyond discussions and professional exchanges, SIMA aims to make creativity a genuine driver of connection across the ecosystem. Through its artist residency, live sessions and immersive formats, the event encourages collaboration between artists, producers, industry professionals and international stakeholders, while creating bridges between African markets and the international creative economy. A Week at the Crossroads of Creativity, Business and Influence From November 7–11, 2026, SIMA Lab. Music will bring together artists and beatmakers from across the continent for an artistic residency designed to produce a collaborative EP, with distribution by an international major label under consideration. On November 12–13, 2026, the professional days and panels will bring together key players from the music ecosystem to explore major issues shaping the future of the industry, including artificial intelligence, copyright, mobility, financing and emerging market opportunities. At the intersection of the cultural and sports industries, a dedicated session will also explore the convergence between football and music, two powerful drivers of influence across the continent, with the participation of sports executives and opinion leaders. As part of this dynamic, Makaya, SIMA’s showcase platform dedicated to discovering new talent, will spotlight emerging artists from Togo, Kenya, Madagascar and other African countries, providing a new stage for the next generation of talent. The programme will also feature the presentation of the Hamed Bakayoko Award, an honorary distinction recognizing the commitment of a patron to the development of Africa’s cultural and creative industries. On November 14, 2026, SIMA will extend the experience through a tourism circuit organized in collaboration with Benin Tourism, inviting artists, professionals and international guests to discover the heritage and iconic sites of Benin. This immersive experience will give participants an opportunity to gain a deeper understanding of the host country’s cultural, historical and tourism assets, while extending networking and exchanges beyond the professional framework of the event. About SIMA Created and initiated by music industry experts, the Francophone African Music Industries Fair (SIMA) promotes the African music industry, provides training and capacity-building opportunities for ecosystem stakeholders, and facilitates business connections between African and international industry players. As a true platform for connecting the cultural and creative industries, SIMA provides ecosystem stakeholders with a space to create, learn, share, connect and foster new collaborations, while contributing to discussions on the cultural, economic and technological issues shaping Africa’s creative industries and their international reach. item.title: Taiwan’s chipmaking giant TSMC to invest $1B in Anthropic, OpenAI
item.description: Top chip manufacturer TSMC is ready to invest $1 billion in Anthropic and OpenAI. That would give the Taiwanese chipmaker direct stakes in leading AI developers, even as its own contract chipmaking business has profited enormously from the AI data center buildout. The chipmaker’s board approved plans to invest up to $500 million in OpenAI preferred stock reserved for large investors and another $500 million to purchase Anthropic common shares at the latter’s expected IPO price, according to Reuters . Such an investment may give markets “a shot of confidence as the artificial-intelligence trade shows signs of strain,” The Wall Street Journal reported. But analysts also warned that such circular financing among investors, suppliers, and customers has made it difficult to evaluate real market demand for AI-related hardware and services, according to the Journal. Read full article Comments

item.title: Trump admin loses fight to spy on random journalists’ LinkedIn DMs
item.description: The Trump administration’s fight to stop suspected leaks of top-secret military information on LinkedIn can’t sweep in “a vast number of confidential sources” of random journalists “who have no conceivable relationship” to the Department of Justice’s investigation, an appeals court ruled Tuesday. The order came after the DOJ asked LinkedIn to turn over 18 months of communications from targeted journalists who collectively published more than 1,000 articles on many different topics over that time period. The request was not limited to journalists involved in a controversial report from a news outlet that Trump said exposed confidential military information in a foreign country. (The outlet is not being named to protect national security secrets.) Instead, the DOJ cast a wide net, requesting extensive LinkedIn data on journalists who had any possible link to the journalists around the time the report was drafted. The majority of journalists have LinkedIn accounts and publish their contact information to encourage sources to connect on the platform, LinkedIn argued. So allowing that government overreach went beyond harming targeted journalists and threatened to undermine a critical platform where journalists frequently connect with confidential sources, judges ruled. Even more concerning, the Trump administration secured a secrecy order barring LinkedIn from telling anyone about the sweeping request for a year. That left journalists unaware for far too long that their First Amendment rights had been compromised, judges ruled. Read full article Comments

item.title: Who will step up to preserve space age artefacts for future generations?
item.description: NASA/JPL-Caltech Around 40,000 years from now, the Voyager 1 probe will pass within astronomical spitting distance of the star Gliese 445. From there, it will continue drifting through the universe on an endless journey that marks humanity’s first attempt to reach the stars. Voyager 1 – which on 18 November will have travelled one light day from Earth – began its odyssey almost 50 years ago, meaning it has been operating for the majority of the space age. That makes it a rarity: most of our iconic spacecraft ended their lives burned up in Earth’s atmosphere or in bits at the bottom of the ocean. Two of the most important missions still flying today, the Hubble Space Telescope and the International Space Station, look set to share the same fate in the near future, even as scientists call for Hubble to be preserved . While some craft like the space shuttles are on display in museums, our present space history is, essentially, in its dark ages, with little thought currently given to preserving spacecraft in situ, where our space-travelling descendants may wish to marvel at them. Even the Apollo hardware left behind on the moon has almost no protection in international law. Advertisement Perhaps we need an organisation like the UNESCO World Heritage Committee to designate important space artefacts for preservation, and encourage funding from cultural and heritage budgets, not scientific ones, to do this. Of course, with such budgets often under threat and the US set to leave UNESCO at the end of this year, this could introduce new problems. Private philanthropy is another option. If humanity is to one day take its place among the stars, a fantasy that fuels many a tech billionaire, it would be a great shame to not be able to look back at how we got there. Just as we remember 19th-century captains of industry like Andrew Carnegie and J. P. Morgan for funding great cultural institutions, perhaps we should be lobbying for the creation of a Musk Space Museum or Bezos Orbital Institute.

item.title: Killer Bigfoot evidence rejected by Bigfoot’s biggest fans
item.description: Josie Ford Feedback is our weekly column of bizarre stories, implausible advertising claims, confusing instructions and more Caught on camera One of the defining features of conspiracy theories is that they are “self-sealing”. If you confront a conspiracy theorist with the lack of evidence for their claim, they will turn this back on you and argue that this very lack of evidence is proof of how powerful the conspiracy is. This is foreshadowing. Advertisement Feedback is interested in watching the new documentary Capturing Bigfoot . We can’t, because we live in the UK and it isn’t available here , but if anyone would care to rectify that, we will stick ourselves in front of it immediately. The film is about the classic footage that purports to show a Bigfoot loping alongside a river in California. Shot by Roger Patterson and Robert Gimlin in 1967, the clip became one of the canonical pieces of evidence for the existence of Bigfoot: a mythical humanoid that supposedly lives in the forests of North America. Bigfoot is one of the icons of cryptozoology, the search for probably-nonexistent creatures. It has hordes of devotees. In Capturing Bigfoot , film-maker Marq Evans uncovers what really happened in 1967. He speaks to Patterson’s associate Bob Heironimus, who says he wore an ape costume in the footage. Crucially, Evans also finds a lost piece of 16-millimetre film, shot in 1966, showing a rehearsal for the final Patterson-Gimlin video. A review of the documentary in Variety calls this footage “the smoking gun”. It is, Feedback would suggest, a case no defence lawyer could wriggle out of. So, the Patterson-Gimlin film purporting to show Bigfoot was fake. Feedback and our editor worried if we were legally safe saying that, but then, as our editor said, “come on”. It is perhaps telling that, when we mentioned this to Mrs Feedback, her response was “I could have sworn I already knew that”. Indeed, these accusations have been made before, notably in Greg Long’s 2004 book The Making of Bigfoot . The new thing is that rehearsal footage. Naturally, then, this footage is what the Bigfoot Field Researchers Organization pushed back on. Its president is quoted in The Times as saying: “My initial reaction is, how could you believe that in the age of AI?… Even if they found some reel, how would you know whether what they’re showing in the documentary is what’s on the reel?” And thus the foreshadowing pays off. item.content:encoded: Josie Ford Feedback is our weekly column of bizarre stories, implausible advertising claims, confusing instructions and more Caught on camera One of the defining features of conspiracy theories is that they are “self-sealing”. If you confront a conspiracy theorist with the lack of evidence for their claim, they will turn this back on you and argue that this very lack of evidence is proof of how powerful the conspiracy is. This is foreshadowing. Advertisement Feedback is interested in watching the new documentary Capturing Bigfoot . We can’t, because we live in the UK and it isn’t available here , but if anyone would care to rectify that, we will stick ourselves in front of it immediately. The film is about the classic footage that purports to show a Bigfoot loping alongside a river in California. Shot by Roger Patterson and Robert Gimlin in 1967, the clip became one of the canonical pieces of evidence for the existence of Bigfoot: a mythical humanoid that supposedly lives in the forests of North America. Bigfoot is one of the icons of cryptozoology, the search for probably-nonexistent creatures. It has hordes of devotees. In Capturing Bigfoot , film-maker Marq Evans uncovers what really happened in 1967. He speaks to Patterson’s associate Bob Heironimus, who says he wore an ape costume in the footage. Crucially, Evans also finds a lost piece of 16-millimetre film, shot in 1966, showing a rehearsal for the final Patterson-Gimlin video. A review of the documentary in Variety calls this footage “the smoking gun”. It is, Feedback would suggest, a case no defence lawyer could wriggle out of. So, the Patterson-Gimlin film purporting to show Bigfoot was fake. Feedback and our editor worried if we were legally safe saying that, but then, as our editor said, “come on”. It is perhaps telling that, when we mentioned this to Mrs Feedback, her response was “I could have sworn I already knew that”. Indeed, these accusations have been made before, notably in Greg Long’s 2004 book The Making of Bigfoot . The new thing is that rehearsal footage. Naturally, then, this footage is what the Bigfoot Field Researchers Organization pushed back on. Its president is quoted in The Times as saying: “My initial reaction is, how could you believe that in the age of AI?… Even if they found some reel, how would you know whether what they’re showing in the documentary is what’s on the reel?” And thus the foreshadowing pays off. A not-so-helpful acronym In late October, a lot of websites suddenly went offline. This was because of a vulnerability in the PHP programming language, which had been known since 2024 but was thought to be too difficult to exploit, until AI tools found how to do it. Reader Chris Hall had never heard of PHP. This seems to have been a common experience: even the BBC’s cyber correspondent Joe Tidy only learned of the existence of PHP when the story broke. Tidy got a lot of online abuse for this, which Feedback thinks is unfair: his job is to explain things clearly, not to be a walking technical manual. In the interests of solidarity, Feedback will say that we still don’t know what distinguishes a baryon from a boson, and at this point we refuse to find out. Anyway, Chris looked up PHP and was given “the helpful information” that it stands for “PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor”. “I can understand the ‘H’ and second ‘P’, ” he says, “but what does the first ‘P’ mean?” Feedback is happy to clarify that PHP originally stood for “personal home page”. When it was upgraded in the late 1990s, the programmers kept the letters and had to think of something new for them to stand for. Hence the recursive backronym that is “PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor”. They just said it Sometimes, scientists fake their results. The problem is spotting the fakery, because it isn’t always obvious. Often, images have been copied from other papers, necessitating systematic searches. Or you have to perform careful statistical analyses on the raw numbers to identify the trends that reveal they have been made up. Or, sometimes, the authors might just flat-out tell you – leaving you to decide whether or not they mean it. Nihar Shah is a computer scientist at Carnegie Mellon University in Pennsylvania, who mostly studies AI scientists: those systems that can do research and write papers with little or no human intervention. However, he is also the author of the blog Research on Research , about “academia, research, and peer review”, where he writes about some of the weird stuff that finds its way into peer-reviewed journals. In October , Shah looked at a host of recent scientific studies and found that many of them included variations on the same phrases. These remarks showed up over and over again, in at least 60 papers . Phrases like: “The values in this table are illustrative placeholders for formatting purposes and must be replaced with results obtained from actual experiments”. Or “Planning scenario, not measured results”. Or “note: the values shown are placeholders and should be replaced with your actual experimental results”. What on Earth is going on? On the face of it, the authors are just admitting that they have made up data. However, Shah says (and Feedback agrees) that there is no reason to assume chicanery. Perhaps all of these papers are built on real results, and the authors just forgot to remove these placeholder texts from early drafts. In other words, this could all be the result of really, really sloppy editing on the part of all concerned. Which is, we guess, reassuring? Um. Got a story for Feedback? You can send stories to Feedback by email at feedback@newscientist.com . Please include your home address. This week’s and past Feedbacks can be seen on our website .

item.title: Ayra Starr Joins Coachella 2027 Lineup Alongside SZA, Dua Lipa & More
item.description: Ayra Starr returns with her third studio album, Starrgirl. Ayra Starr is taking her global run to another big stage! The Nigerian singer has been named among the performers at Coachella 2027, adding another major festival appearance to her growing list of international milestones. The Beninese-born singer, who rose to prominence as one of Afrobeats’ leading voices after joining Mavin Records, is set to perform on both weekends of the festival, Sunday, April 11, and Sunday, April 18, 2027. Coachella will take place at the Empire Polo Club in Indio, California. It’s been a big year for Ayra, with her third studio album, Starrgirl, adding to an already exciting run. Fans heading to the festival can look forward to hearing songs from the project, including “ Tornado ” and “ Midnight in New York “, as well as her collaboration “ Gimme Dat “. There’s also room for crowd favourites such as “ Rush “, “ Commas ” and “ Heaven Baby “. Ayra shares the Sunday bill with headliner SZA , alongside Victoria Monét , Jorja Smith , Becky G and Don Toliver . The wider festival, running from April 9 to 11 and April 16 to 18, will also feature headliners Dua Lipa and Tame Impala , with Madonna set for a special appearance in the dance tent. Her Coachella booking follows another major moment in London, where she performed at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium as part of the NFL International Games halftime show, becoming the first African artist to headline the show. And there’s even more for fans to look forward to. Ayra has announced her 20-city Starrgirl World Tour , which will take her across Europe and North America in early 2027 before she heads to the California desert for Coachella. What a year ahead for the Starr girl. The official Coachella 2027 lineup featuring Nigerian singer Ayra Starr alongside headliners Dua Lipa, Tame Impala, and SZA at the Empire Polo Club in Indio, California. item.title: US bit barn boom sees energy needs grow 10x as fast as grid capacity
item.description: Datacenter power consumption in the US is growing roughly ten times faster than grid capacity, meaning facilities may soon need to find a large chunk of their own electricity from other sources. Surging demand for AI infrastructure is driving a wave of new server farms across America, but it is exposing long-term underinvestment in the grid networks required to deliver power where it's needed. Insurance broker Howden calculates that datacenters would need to source up to 58 percent of their power off the grid by 2030 just to keep their share of grid capacity from growing. Gartner warned in June that the energy consumed by AI datacenters is on track to grow 26 percent this year, and grid supply may be unable to keep pace with demand by the end of this decade. Howden's analysis of data from the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) and S&P Global found that since the year 2000, power being fed to data campuses has risen 19 percent a year on average, while the electricity grid expanded capacity by just 2 percent per annum over the same period. Datacenters' share of US grid capacity was circa five percent in 2025, up from 0.1 percent in 2000 – a 50-fold increase. Management consultancy Bain & Company issued a report two years ago warning that energy companies must switch gear and invest in building out grid capacity faster , as energy draw by server farms is expected to more than double by 2030. This doesn't mean that datacenters are in danger of eating all of America's electricity, at least not in the immediate future. The graph makes it appear that the two lines are about to cross, but the chart uses different scales: 1,400 gigawatts on the left axis for grid capacity, versus just 80 on the right for datacenters. Keeping datacenters at five percent of grid capacity requires 110 gigawatts of behind-the-meter capacity by 2030, Howden estimates – an expansion it considers unlikely. Instead, it expects a combination of greater reliance on the grid, slower development at power-constrained sites, and alternative supplies. For the largest, most power-constrained projects, Howden warns that grid delays of two to six years could mean $800 million to $2.4 billion in forgone revenue. "Power availability is becoming one of the defining challenges of the datacenter boom," says Howden head of Natural Resources Stuart Adam. "As demand for AI infrastructure accelerates, developers are increasingly looking beyond traditional grid connections to secure the electricity they need." Howden's business is insurance, and so Adam also notes that on-site generation introduces new operational and financial exposures, as operators take greater responsibility for their power infrastructure. ®

item.title: Big Walk used AI to fix a bug. Now the indie gaming world is having a reckoning.
item.description: The last few years have seen significant debate over the widespread use of AI-powered tools in game development and the responsible disclosure of that usage to players. That debate has exploded into a full-blown controversy in the indie game development space this week, as Big Walk developer House House has publicly and belatedly disclosed minimal AI use in its popular co-operative puzzle exploration game. This particular controversy has been brewing behind the scenes for months, as judges and jury members for the prestigious Independent Games Festival Awards discussed the issue in private discussion groups. But the debate started to break into public view on Monday when 19 members of the 50-plus-member jury released a signed statement outlining a stance "declining to vote for any game that uses generative AI in any capacity." Noting "a significant increase in the number of submitted games developer with generative AI tools," the group of jurors called out AI's ecological, economic, psychological, and labor harms in rejecting tools whose use, they said, is still "not a foregone conclusion in our industry." Read full article Comments

item.title: Toyota’s Scion is back, starting with an American-made, 25-mph kei truck
item.description: Toyota is dusting off the Scion badge for a radically different mission. Rather than targeting youth-market hatchbacks, "Scion by Toyota" is being positioned as an experimental mobility incubator - and its first vehicle is an authentic Japanese-style kei truck built in Indiana. Kei vehicles, which are built to satisfy Japan's light vehicle regulations, are enjoying surging popularity around the world, including here in the US. item.title: Apple is shuttering its 28-year-old online community forum
item.description: Apple’s online community forum will close on November 20. On Tuesday night, Apple posted a message to the Apple Support Community announcing the forum's closure: The Apple Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state. You can continue to find trusted guidance and support on the official Apple Support site . We want to thank the community members who have contributed their time and expertise to help others with their Apple products. For 28 years, the forum has provided Apple users with a way to get quick technical advice about their products. That advice usually came from fellow users, though Apple employees occasionally chimed in. As with any community forum, the helpfulness and accuracy of the advice varied. Read full article Comments

item.title: Scientists check their work and confirm it with update on iconic black hole image
item.description: The image of the red ring around the black hole M87, produced by the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) array, made front-page news around the world in 2019. There was one problem: there was a slim chance the depiction might be wrong. This week, a small team of four Australian researchers have published their work confirming the result based on a new machine learning algorithm using the same base data. The 2019 Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) image came from hundreds of scientists working together to capture the first direct view of a black hole's shadow. The measurements were taken at eight telescopes around the world, at locations including Chile, the US, and Antarctica. Reconstructing the image from the data so geographically distant meant instrument and environment errors could influence the accuracy of the resulting image. Potentially, alternative analyses of the data could have reconstructed an image without the iconic ring shape. Samuel Lai – a postdoctoral fellow at the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO) in Western Australia – and his team created an independent imaging algorithm to process the historic dataset to validate the result. The new approach used closed triplets (using three telescopes for error correction) rather than station pairs in an effort to reduce error. To the relief of the EHT team, the new image recreated the iconic ring-like image seen in the original, according to a paper published in Nature today . In a prepared statement, Lai said taking pictures of black holes was not easy. "It is like standing in your backyard and trying to take a photo of a doughnut on the Moon," he said. He explained that when his team applied new advanced machine learning and artificial intelligence techniques to the original Event Horizon Telescope dataset, they found a black hole almost identical in size and shape to the historic EHT image. "Importantly, our model had no idea what a black hole looked like when we applied it to the M87 data. This is the first truly independent validation of the EHT image, an important step in the scientific process," he said. Event Horizon Telescope director Laurent Loinard welcomed the new study. "It is extremely gratifying to see that an elegant, entirely independent method recovers the ring structure of M87 across several years, in excellent agreement with the EHT Collaboration's published results," he said. ®

item.title: Did comets bring building blocks of life to Earth? Scientists aren't so sure anymore
item.description: The origin of life on Earth remains a mystery. New research shows that comets almost certainly did not bring the chemical building blocks of life to our planet. Life as we know it is based around carbon chemistry, also known as organic chemistry. Complex organic molecules are the fundamental building blocks of biochemical compounds such as nucleobases, amino acids, sugars and so on that act as the machinery for biochemistry on Earth . Two big questions are where did this complex chemistry originate? Did these complex organic molecules form on Earth, or were they delivered here from space? New research led by planetary scientist Richard Anslow of the Institute for Astronomy at the University of Cambridge has now seemingly ruled out comets as the origin of complex organic molecules on Earth. "Historically, scientists thought that comets were important for the origin of life on Earth, because they carried carbon and nitrogen-bearing molecules, so these giant space snowballs were almost like a 'get-out-of-jail-free card' that brought all the molecules a planet would need to seed life," said Anslow in a statement . Stripping the romance from the Earth's turbulent past Comet impacts on Earth were much more frequent in the first half-billion years of the solar system ’s existence, when there were still lots of debris leftover from the formation of the planets. For over a century comet impacts had been considered a prime suspect in the search for what brought the building blocks of life to Earth. However, while comets bringing the building blocks of life to Earth is "kind of a romantic idea," according to Anslow, the University of Cambridge researcher added that the team's results suggest that is highly unlikely. Anslow and colleagues arrived at this conclusion based upon computer modeling by using the very latest simulations depicting the origin and evolution of comets and their orbits, their interactions with Earth's atmosphere as they enter it, and of the hypervelocity comet impacts themselves. In particular, they used the fate of hydrogen cyanide as a proxy for what happens to complex organic molecules in comet impacts. Hydrogen cyanide is frequently found in comets and was even detected in the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS . An artist’s impression of a comet crashing into the early Earth (Image credit: Scarlett White) The problem is that comets are generally moving at too great a velocity. For organic molecules to survive impact, the impact velocity would have to be below 33,500 miles per hour (15 kilometers per second). Anslow and his colleagues found that, in general, comets travel too fast and enter Earth’s atmosphere at too sharp an angle for complex organic molecules to survive. Instead, they are mostly vaporized on impact. item.dc:creator: Keith Cooper
item.content:encoded: The origin of life on Earth remains a mystery. New research shows that comets almost certainly did not bring the chemical building blocks of life to our planet. Life as we know it is based around carbon chemistry, also known as organic chemistry. Complex organic molecules are the fundamental building blocks of biochemical compounds such as nucleobases, amino acids, sugars and so on that act as the machinery for biochemistry on Earth . Two big questions are where did this complex chemistry originate? Did these complex organic molecules form on Earth, or were they delivered here from space? New research led by planetary scientist Richard Anslow of the Institute for Astronomy at the University of Cambridge has now seemingly ruled out comets as the origin of complex organic molecules on Earth. "Historically, scientists thought that comets were important for the origin of life on Earth, because they carried carbon and nitrogen-bearing molecules, so these giant space snowballs were almost like a 'get-out-of-jail-free card' that brought all the molecules a planet would need to seed life," said Anslow in a statement . Stripping the romance from the Earth's turbulent past Comet impacts on Earth were much more frequent in the first half-billion years of the solar system ’s existence, when there were still lots of debris leftover from the formation of the planets. For over a century comet impacts had been considered a prime suspect in the search for what brought the building blocks of life to Earth. However, while comets bringing the building blocks of life to Earth is "kind of a romantic idea," according to Anslow, the University of Cambridge researcher added that the team's results suggest that is highly unlikely. Anslow and colleagues arrived at this conclusion based upon computer modeling by using the very latest simulations depicting the origin and evolution of comets and their orbits, their interactions with Earth's atmosphere as they enter it, and of the hypervelocity comet impacts themselves. In particular, they used the fate of hydrogen cyanide as a proxy for what happens to complex organic molecules in comet impacts. Hydrogen cyanide is frequently found in comets and was even detected in the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS . An artist’s impression of a comet crashing into the early Earth (Image credit: Scarlett White) The problem is that comets are generally moving at too great a velocity. For organic molecules to survive impact, the impact velocity would have to be below 33,500 miles per hour (15 kilometers per second). Anslow and his colleagues found that, in general, comets travel too fast and enter Earth’s atmosphere at too sharp an angle for complex organic molecules to survive. Instead, they are mostly vaporized on impact. Even on the rare occasions that the complex organic molecules survived, they were usually not in great enough abundance to provide any meaningful prebiotic chemistry. "It would really have to be a one-in-a-million occurrence, because not only would you need an impact at just the right speed and just the right angle, you would also need everything to happen after that point, in terms of the concentration and the speed at which the chemical origins of life got going," said Anslow. "We can’t rule out for certain that it happened that way, but it seems to be a really rare occurrence – at best, a one-off fluke." Maybe life on Earth is a fluke It is not yet known if the origin of life on Earth was a fluke, or whether life is plentiful in the universe, so a fluke occurrence could still have been a trigger for life on our planet. However, researchers are coming around to alternatives, either that all the pre-biotic chemistry that resulted in life took place on Earth without requiring material from space, or asteroids instead brought those important molecules to Earth. Scientists have found asteroids to be rich in those molecules – for example, the sample of material brought back by the OSIRIS-REx mission from the near-Earth asteroid Bennu contained all the building blocks of RNA. However, other planets could have plausibly benefitted from comet impacts. The simulations showed that complex organic molecules in comets would stand a slightly better chance of surviving impacts on Mars , because of the Red Planet’s thinner atmosphere and lower gravity. "This is not to say it definitely happened on Mars, of course, but it suggests it would be unlikely if it happened on Earth and didn’t happen on Mars," said Anslow. "Or the other, perhaps more likely, alternative is that it didn’t happen on either planet." The 7 planets circling the star TRAPPIST-1, 3 of which might be able to keep liquid water on its surface. (Image credit: R. Hurt/T. Pyle/NASA) More intriguing are the possibilities on exoplanets, specifically the peas-in-a-pod multi-planet systems around red dwarf stars such as TRAPPIST-1 , where all the planets are bunched up close. In 2023 Anslow wrote a research paper describing how comets could gravitationally bounce from one planet to the next, losing velocity in the process so that when they crash into one of the planets, they impact is not so severe and complex organic molecules might have a chance to survive. The team's research was published on 28 October in Scientific Reports .

item.title: Canonical web services get stage fright ahead of Ubuntu Summit
item.description: A swathe of Canonical's web services has been offline for hours, an awkward warm-up for tomorrow's Ubuntu Summit. Canonical's status page lists widespread disruption beginning at approximately 1100 UTC, affecting gopkg.in, Ubuntu cloud images and mailing lists, jaas.ai, the Ubuntu keyserver, Launchpad PPAs, the Livepatch API, canonical.com, Ubuntu login, maas.io, and 16 other services. Landscape is also affected. Email and the company's Discourse forums remain available. The Register has asked Canonical for more information but had received no response at publication time. The company suffered a DDoS attack last month , although the cause of this outage has not been confirmed. The timing is unfortunate. As the banner across the top of the Discourse forum page says: "The Ubuntu Summit starts tomorrow – join from anywhere!" The online event runs on November 12-13. For the first time since the 2022 Summit in Prague, The Reg FOSS desk won't be attending in person. Canonical is still experimenting with the format of the event, and the last few have been primarily online, with just a small in-person audience in its London offices. This is the second of two Summits this year, labeled 26.04 and 26.10 to mirror Ubuntu's release cycle. The timetable , hosted on the Discourse site, lists several talks on AI and agentic coding. The AI-heavy program we reported from June's event appears to be continuing. ®

item.title: IBM to offer access to a dual-processor quantum system in 2027
item.description: IBM's Quantum Developer's Conference is being held this week, and the company is using the gathering to provide an update to its roadmap: It is aiming to make error-corrected quantum computers before the decade is out. The changes greatly expand the scope of its next-generation Nighthawk general-use processors by adding a version with over 500 programmable qubits. At the same time, it's stepping back a bit on its plan to link multiple Nighthawk processors together, dropping the intended number of linked systems from nine to two. The total number of qubits planned for next year will remain the same; how the company is getting there, however, will be different. Read full article Comments

item.title: Top four teams in Fifa rankings set to be kept apart until semi-finals at 2027 Women’s World Cup
item.description: Team must win World Cup group to trigger rule Spain, US, Germany and England currently in top four The top four ranked teams will be separated until the semi-finals at the 2027 Women’s World Cup, ­provided they each win their group, after a change to the tournament’s draw procedure was confirmed by Fifa. Spain, USA, Germany and England are ranked one to four in the world respectively, although USA and England still need to qualify for the tournament. The seedings will be based on the 7 December updated rankings, meaning the standings could change before the draw, which will take place on 11 December in Rio de Janeiro. Continue reading...

item.title: 'There's tremendous demand': Rocket Lab raises price of Neutron launch from $55 million to $70 million
item.description: null The coming launch bottleneck has ramped up demand for a rocket that has yet to leave the ground. Rocket Lab announced on Monday (Nov. 9) that it recently raised the price of a Neutron launch from $55 million to $70 million — an increase of more than 25%, for a ride on a rocket that's set to debut in 2027. "Launch is extremely constrained, and that is exactly the situation we predicted," Rocket Lab founder and CEO Peter Beck said on Monday during the company's third-quarter earnings call. "We saw a pent-up launch market on the horizon, and rather than provide early discounted launches, we set out to deliver a rocket into an environment with extreme demand at full price or higher." Rocket Lab is best known for Electron , a workhorse small-satellite launcher that debuted in 2017 and now has 90 orbital missions under its belt. The 59-foot-tall (18 meters) expendable rocket and can haul 660 pounds (300 kilograms) to low Earth orbit (LEO). Neutron is the company's entry into the medium-lift market. It features a reusable first stage, stands 141 feet (43 m) tall and can carry 14.3 tons (13 metric tons) of payload to LEO. Rocket Lab announced Neutron back in 2021 and first targeted a 2024 debut for the vehicle. But various problems have cropped up over the years, pushing things back. Last month, for example, Rocket Lab announced that it was delaying the first Neutron flight from late 2026 into 2027 due to a manufacturing issue (which it says is now under control). Such setbacks have not dampened demand for Neutron's services, however. During Monday's call, Beck revealed that Rocket Lab booked eight Neutron launches during the third quarter of 2026, which ran from July 1 through Sept. 30. The contracts for those eight flights are worth "a total of roughly 515 million, including multiple missions on a new escalated base price of $70 million," Beck said. Neutron's first 16 launches are now sold out, he added, and bookings from here on will be for flights in the 2030s. "The demand is a function of both a tightening global launch supply and our customers' confidence that Rocket Lab is the right partner to break the world's launch bottleneck," Beck said. Artist's illustration of Neutron's first stage coming down for a landing on a ship at sea. (Image credit: Rocket Lab) That bottleneck is coming in 2028 or so, when SpaceX plans to retire its Falcon 9 rocket . For some perspective, and comparison with Neutron: SpaceX currently charges $74 million for each Falcon 9 launch. The rocket has a reusable first stage and can carry about 25 tons (22.7 metric tons) to LEO. The medium lifter has been the world's most prolific rocket for the past few years. In 2025, for example, it flew 165 times — roughly the same number of orbital missions as all other launchers in the world combined. And all 165 of those flights were successful.
