And they're looking to the next generation for help, the space agency's chief Jared Isaacman said Sunday (Nov. 8). "We are inviting students from across the country to help solve some of the problems that stand between humanity and a permanent presence on another world," Isaacman said. "We're putting 1 million in prizes together to support the best ideas and recognize the teams behind them." Isaacman made this announcement wearing his blue flight suit from the rocket garden at NASA's Kennedy Space Center Visitor Center amidst the agency's MAX POWER air show event . Just the day before, he flew fighter jets in that suit and even jumped out of a plane, skydiving into the event. Soon after this announcement, he was flying another fighter plane above the crowd. The audience for this announcement was filled with students of all ages. Some young children wearing costume spacesuits squeezed as close as they could to the front of the room while teenagers considering their futures listened intently. It was clear that Isaacman's presence and words were landing with this group. But what moon base challenges does NASA want to see these students tackle? In short, all of them. "The moon base will allow us to conduct groundbreaking science, test new technologies, and prepare again for where we inevitably go next, which is the red planet," he said. "But before any of that can happen, we have an awful lot of problems that need to be solved." "We need ways to generate power through the long lunar night . We need to protect our astronauts from that incredibly harsh and dangerous and demanding environment on the surface. We need to move people and equipment around on the surface and support human life three days away from Earth," Isaacman said, illustrating just a few of the big issues that present with the concept of a moon base. NASA Adminisrator Jared Isaacman invites students to help NASA build a moon base at NASA's Kennedy Space Center Visitor Center. (Image credit: Chelsea Gohd) How will it work? This challenge is open to high school and post-secondary students based in the U.S. For participating students, they will form teams that will work on an idea from one of six different technical topics related to creating and running a moon base. These six topics include power systems, habitats, communications, mobility, life support and astronaut safety . This will be what Isaacman described as a "multi-phase competition that mirrors how ideas are developed actually in the aerospace industry." "Teams will first submit concepts, then they're going to refine them, and finalists will have the opportunity to present their solutions directly to NASA leaders and stakeholders," he further explained. "The prize money is great for sure, but the the real opportunity is to work on problems NASA is actively trying to solve right now, so students don't need to wait to graduation to contribute to that effort," Isaacman added. A long road ahead Right now, NASA has a long road ahead of them before a moon base is actually built. In mid-2027, the agency is planning to launch its Artemis III mission which will see a crew of four astronauts practice rendezvous maneuvers with two different lunar landers. If all goes to plan, this will be followed by Artemis IV landing humans on the moon's surface for the first time since the final Apollo mission in 1972. The agency is making these big steps forward to not just a crewed return to the moon, but a sustained, long-term return to the moon. However, knowing that a fully-fledged moon base is still firmly in the future, they are banking on the ingenuity, creativity and passion of If you're a student or know a student interested in participating in this challenge, you can find more information on NASA's website here . Interested students can register until Jan. 25, 2027.

item.title: Netflix announces 'Stranger Things' spin-off 'Other Worlds', and it's already teasing a trip to Area 51 (video)
item.description: null So, you thought "Stranger Things" was done and dusted after all that Conformity Gate nonsense? No way! Netflix's sci-fi sensation returns in the live-action prequel series "Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure." Created by the Duffer Brothers and Kate Trefry, with the episodes set to be directed by Joe Wright ("Darkest Hour", "Black Mirror"), this new show isn't set in Hawkins or the electric '80s. No, this time around, the action takes place in Marion, Nevada, in 1955, and you know what else is located in Nevada, right? Area 51 . The teaser trailer certainly teases the possibility of a trip to the world's most paradoxically famous secret military base, showcasing a bike and radio resting outside of a fence with a sign that clearly says it's a restricted area (in any TV show or film, that's actually an invitation to see what's on the other side). Of course, the tease doesn't end there, as the thunder booms in the sky and there's a visual hint of a wormhole. No story details about "Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure" have been released to date, but there are some clues out there for all the Internet sleuths. Trefrey wrote the Henry Creel-focused "Stranger Things: The First Shadow" play, while Matt Duffer explained to Variety how a spin-off show would tackle the rock that Henry found in the briefcase in "Stranger Things." So, yes, expect this to be a Henry-centric affair and the start of his long, hard road to hell and becoming Vecna. (Image credit: Netflix) What'll be interesting, though, is to see how the show ties into the history of Area 51. After all, it was on April 12, 1955, that CIA officer Richard Bissell discovered the site, while the "Other Worlds" trailer has the date of April 19th clearly marked onscreen, so the timelines align nicely here. "Stranger Things" has never been shy of tying itself to real-world science and historical events, so it'll be fascinating to see how the show explores Area 51 as a concept and the secrets everybody believes are hidden there. Was it really a site to test highly advanced weapons and aircraft, or was E.T. 's cousin held hostage there until he revealed Colonel Sanders' 11 herbs and spices? Who knows, with all this renewed excitement around this mysterious military facility, we might get another "Storm Area 51" event to enjoy and laugh at all over again. Regardless, more "Stranger Things" is welcome news, and since it's presumably about one of the show's best characters, Henry Creel, it only adds another layer to his already intriguing lore. If we can't have an origin story about Hopper's incredible and envious moustache, this is the next best thing. "Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure" arrives on Netflix in 2028. item.title: Football Daily | Manchester United, Aston Villa and the unseriousness of a 4-4 draw
item.description: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! Precisely 13,266 games have been played since the inception of the Premier League, and 19 of those matches have finished 4-4 (0.1%), a rarity in a division dominated by the mighty 1-0 (17.6%). It was about time we got one, though. The months of August and September, when teams are still fighting to define their top-flight seasons and fitness and motivation tend to be at their peak, have never seen a single 4-4 draw. As motivation decreases the chances of stupid scorelines increase, and that’s where the 4-4 creeps in. There’s a certain on-the-beachness inherent in the score, and it is no coincidence that it has occurred more in the second half of April, as thoughts drift to the close season and the ineffable pointlessness of a lot of late-campaign football becomes unavoidable, than in the entirety of any other month. Students, teachers and visitors at the University of Queensland can view the world’s longest-running experiment. The flamin’ pitch drop experiment began in 1930 and is designed to demonstrate how an apparent solid (pitch) behaves like an extremely viscous liquid. Nearly 100 years ago pitch was placed in a funnel and kept at room temperature. It moves incredibly slowly at a rate of approximately one atom per second (slower than the continental drift), and only nine drips have ever been recorded , though never witnessed. Without the need for intercontinental travel, perhaps other readers can now appreciate what it’s like to watch Arsenal win 1-0 ” – John Holtom. Continue reading...

item.title: Carex Rewards Consumers As Everybody Wins Promo Concludes With Grand Finale Live Draw
item.description: Carex, one of Nigeria’s leading personal hygiene brands, has successfully concluded its nationwide Everybody Wins Promo with a transparent Grand Finale Live Draw , rewarding loyal consumers and reinforcing its commitment to delivering value beyond personal care products. The campaign, which ran from June 2026 to August 2026, attracted millions of consumers PAN Nigeria and rewarded winners with prizes worth over ₦400,000,000. The Grand Finale Live Draw, held in Lagos, brought together consumers, media representatives, trade partners, regulatory officials, and other key stakeholders to witness the selection of the campaign’s grand prize winner through a transparent and independently supervised process. The event marked the culmination of months of consumer participation and engagement, further strengthening the connection between the Carex brand and its consumers. Throughout the promotion, participants had multiple opportunities to win exciting rewards, including instant Recharge Cards, shopping Vouchers, and a brand-new Car. Over 90,000 consumers emerged as winners over the course of the campaign. The grand prize car winner, Faith Stephen from Ijebu Ode, Ogun State, emerged through the live draw process conducted in accordance with all applicable promotional and regulatory requirements. Speaking at the event, Ifunanya Anwunah , Head of Category – Personal Hygiene, said: “At Carex, we believe that the consumers who trust our products every day deserve to be appreciated and rewarded. The Everybody Wins Promo was created as a tangible expression of our gratitude for the loyalty and support we continue to receive from Nigerian families. “ The overwhelming participation and enthusiasm witnessed throughout this campaign demonstrate the strong connection consumers have with the Carex brand. The promo was built on a simple promise: giving everyday consumers the opportunity to win meaningful rewards while enjoying the quality, care, and protection they have come to trust from Carex. As a brand trusted by millions of Nigerians for their personal hygiene and care needs, Carex remains committed to developing initiatives that deepen consumer engagement, reward loyalty, and create memorable experiences for consumers across the country. The successful completion of the Everybody Wins Promo further underscores the brand’s commitment to putting consumers at the heart of everything it does. About Carex Carex is committed to winning the war against germs through a range of antibacterial products that support the health, hygiene, and wellbeing of consumers. Through innovative products and engaging consumer initiatives, Carex continues to build meaningful connections with families across Nigeria, delivering trusted products that help consumers live healthier and more confident lives. The Everybody Wins Promo was created as a tangible expression of our gratitude for the loyalty and support we continue to receive from Nigerian families. “ The overwhelming participation and enthusiasm witnessed throughout this campaign demonstrate the strong connection consumers have with the Carex brand. The promo was built on a simple promise: giving everyday consumers the opportunity to win meaningful rewards while enjoying the quality, care, and protection they have come to trust from Carex. As a brand trusted by millions of Nigerians for their personal hygiene and care needs, Carex remains committed to developing initiatives that deepen consumer engagement, reward loyalty, and create memorable experiences for consumers across the country. The successful completion of the Everybody Wins Promo further underscores the brand’s commitment to putting consumers at the heart of everything it does. item.title: Manchester City’s weaknesses under Enzo Maresca are being exposed
item.description: After three straight defeats, City’s manager says he will use the international break to reassess. Their problems may go beyond tactics Sign up for our free newsletter here Enzo Maresca seemed, if not quite baffled by his side’s Saturday defeat to Nottingham Forest, then at least a little put out. After seven straight wins from the start of the season, that’s now three straight defeats, a pattern so unusual that it’s been recorded only once before in top-flight English history, by Sheffield Wednesday in 1904-05. The three defeats were all different, Maresca said, although in all of them City had had more possession and more chances. In the 2-1 defeat at Aston Villa two weeks ago, City had 63% of the ball and had 15 chances to Villa’s eight. In the 1-0 home defeat to Brighton last weekend, they had 62% possession and 21 chances to seven. At the City Ground, it was 79% possession and 12 chances to 11. So Maresca is right in one way: City could look at basic statistics and say they had been unfortunate – although Forest could equally point to the fact that they went into that game third top of the expected goals table but second-bottom of the actual table. This is an extract from Soccer Desk, a newsletter from the Guardian US. Subscribe for free here . Continue reading...

item.title: NASA needs more astronauts for moon missions and beyond. You can apply now, but only until Dec. 3
item.description:
Tariq is the Editor-in-Chief of Space.com based out of our New York City office and joined the team in 2001, first as an intern and staff writer, and later as an editor. He covers human spaceflight, exploration and space science, as well as skywatching and entertainment. He became Space.com's Managing Editor in 2009 and Editor-in-Chief in 2019. In October 2022, Tariq received the Harry Kolcum Award for excellence in space reporting from the National Space Club Florida Committee. In June 2025, the National Space Society awarded him the Space Pioneer Award for Excellence in Mass Media at the International Space Development Conference in Orlando, Florida.

Hailing from Stockton, California (where he attended the same high school as NASA astronaut Jose Hernandez), Tariq studied print journalism and astronomy at the University of Southern California in Los Angeles, earning a bachelor's degree in journalism in 1999 along with a minor in astronomy. He then served as a staff reporter for The Los Angeles Times covering education and city beats in La Habra and Fullerton in Orange County for the Our Times sections.

In 2000, Tariq became the city reporter for the Huntington Beach Independent, a weekly publication of the Los Angeles Times, covering local politics and events, crime, business and environmental issues. He left the Los Angeles Times in 2001 to study science journalism at New York University, where he earned a master's degree in 2002 from NYU's Science and Environmental Reporting Program (now the Science, Health and Environmental Reporting Program) under the direction of space reporter William Burrows.

Tariq first joined Space.com as an intern in September 2001 while also serving as a research assistant for nutrition writer Gary Taubes and writing freelance projects, where his work appeared in The Scientist and Laboratory Equipment Magazine. He became a full-time reporter covering spaceflight in 2004, with this first launch being NASA's STS-114 Return to Flight mission in July 2005.

Tariq is also an Eagle Scout (yes, he has the Space Exploration merit badge) and went to Space Camp four times as a kid and a fifth time as an adult. When not writing about space, you can find Tariq watching the latest Star Trek TV series, sci-fi movies and reading about hippos, his favorite animal. You can find Tariq at Space.com and as the co-host to the This Week In Space podcast with space historian Rod Pyle on the TWiT network. To see his latest project, you can follow Tariq on Twitter @tariqjmalik.

If NASA ever hopes to build a permanent moon base for astronauts, let alone aim for Mars, the U.S. space agency is going to need a whole lot of space travelers. And now, you have a chance to be one of them. NASA on Saturday (Nov. 7) put out the call for a new class of astronaut candidates who think they have the "right stuff" to fly, live and work in space. Those astronaut hopefuls have until Dec. 3 to apply ( the application website is here ), with NASA planning to make its final selections in late 2027. "This is an extraordinary time to join NASA's astronaut corps," the space agency's chief, Jared Isaacman, said in an announcement , which was made during NASA's "Max Power" air show at Kennedy Space Center (KSC) in Florida. "The people we select could walk on the moon, live and work at the Moon Base , and help pioneer the systems and operations that will ultimately carry crews to Mars." It's been two years since NASA last sought applications for astronauts. In 2024, more than 8,000 people applied, though only 10 — five men and five women — made the cut. They're in the middle of a two-year training program right now. This new 2027 astronaut group will be the 25th astronaut class in NASA history. Its announcement comes the same year that NASA returned astronauts to the moon for the first time since the Apollo era with the Artemis II moon flyby . Four more astronauts will test Artemis moon landers in Earth orbit on the Artemis III mission in 2027. NASA currently has 32 active astronauts in its spaceflying corps. The agency has recruited 370 people to fly in space since 1959, when the first seven Mercury astronauts were selected and unveiled to the world. "There is a lot to be done in order to get all of these new vehicles and the new suits and everything as we continue to work towards the moon, build a base there, stay permanently, and then eventually onto Mars ," NASA astronaut Nichole Stilwell, class of 2021, told Space.com in an interview at KSC during the Max Power event. "And so we just don't have enough people, and we're looking for more." NASA's 2025 astronaut class, as seen in September 2025 when NASA announced them to the world. They are: U.S. Army CW3 Ben Bailey, U.S. Air Force Maj. Cameron Jones, Katherine Spies, Anna Menon, U.S. Navy Lt. Cmdr. Erin Overcash, U.S. Air Force Maj. Adam Fuhrmann, Dr. Lauren Edgar, Yuri Kubo, Rebecca Lawler, and Dr. Imelda Muller. (Image credit: NASA) If you're interested in applying to be a NASA astronaut , you should take a look at the requirements first. NASA's core guidelines require applicants to be U.S. citizens and have a master's degree in a STEM field like "engineering, biological science, physical science, or computer science from an accredited institution," the space agency said in a statement. You'll also need at least three years of experience in your related field. Don't have a master's degree? Here's three other ways NASA might consider your application, according to the agency's advisory : "Completion of at least two years of work toward a doctoral program in an appropriate technical field of engineering, biological science, physical science, computer science, or mathematics. "Completion of a Doctor of Medicine, Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine, Physician Assistant, Doctor of Nursing Practice, Family Nurse Practitioner, or a related medical degree. "Completion of, or current enrollment in, a nationally recognized Test Pilot School program, provided the program is completed by July 2027. If Test Pilot School is the only advanced technical degree, then completion of a bachelor’s degree in a STEM field, including engineering, biological science, physical science, or computer science is required." If you're a medical doctor and are considering applying to be an astronaut, your residency training can be counted toward your professional experience, but only if it is completed by July 2027, NASA said. If you want to be a pilot astronaut for NASA, you'll need some serious flight hours under your belt. Here's a rundown of some ways to meet that requirement: 750 hours flying as pilot in command of high-performance jet aircraft. 1,000 total flight hours in a rotary-wing aircraft, with 300 hours as pilot in command. 1,500 total flight hours in other fixed-wing aircraft, with 750 hours as pilot in command. "For those who apply, becoming a NASA astronaut is more than a career opportunity,” said NASA chief astronaut Scott Tingle, who also chairs the Astronaut Selection Board at the agency's Johnson Space Center (JSC) in Houston. "It is a chance to join a legacy of explorers who have pushed the boundaries of discovery and play a role in the missions that will shape humanity’s future in space." Once NASA selects its 2027 astronaut class, the new recruits can expect to begin a two-year training program based out of JSC, which is home to the agency's astronaut corp and Mission Control. “The window is open. The mission is waiting.," NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson said in a statement. "And the only thing missing from the greatest adventure humanity has ever embarked upon is you." Space.com Content Manager Chelsea Gohd contributed to this report from NASA's Max Power event at the Kennedy Spa

item.title: Futuristic aircraft takes flight at NASA | Space photo of the day for Nov. 9, 2026
item.description: null The future of flight meets space exploration as a futuristic electric aircraft hovers beside Blue Origin's massive New Glenn rocket stage. (Image credit: Chelsea Gohd/Future) A futuristic single-person aircraft takes to the skies at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, with the upper stage of Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket providing a dramatic backdrop. The unusual scene was captured during the MAX POWER event, which brought together innovators and emerging technologies at the iconic spaceflight facility. What is it? The photograph shows a single-person electric aircraft called Jetson ONE, developed by Jetson, a US-based company working to bring personal flight to the skies. The compact rotorcraft uses multiple propellers to climb into the air, allowing it to take off and vertically without the need for a runway. The aircraft was performing flight demonstrations during the UP.Summit gathering, which formed part of the larger MAX POWER event at the Kennedy Space Center. During the demonstrations, the Jetson ONE demonstrated its ability to maneuver through the air and hover in place, giving spectators a close-up look at the technology in action. Jetson ONE demonstration at MAX POWER. (Image credit: Chelsea Gohd/Future) Why is it amazing? The photograph offers a fascinating glimpse at two very different approaches to flight. While Jetson is developing small electric aircraft designed for personal transportation, Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket is built to carry payloads far beyond Earth's atmosphere.

item.title: SpaceX will launch epic double-catch Starship Flight 15 test mission on Nov. 13
item.description: null SpaceX will make spaceflight history this week, if all goes according to plan. The company announced over the weekend that it's targeting Friday (Nov. 13) for the 15th test flight of its Starship megarocket, which will attempt something that's never been done before. "The upcoming flight is planned to be the first to return both Starship and Super Heavy to the launch site for catch," SpaceX wrote in a description of Flight 15 . "If successful, this will mark the first full recovery of an orbital launch system and a breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket." SpaceX's Starship megarocket launches on its 14th test flight on Sept. 28, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX) Super Heavy is Starship's giant booster, and Starship (or Ship for short) is its upper-stage spacecraft. As SpaceX's description noted, both elements are designed to be fully and rapidly reusable. "Catch" refers to SpaceX's recovery mechanism for both stages: Each will return to the launch mount at SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas and be plucked out of the sky by the tower's "chopstick" arms. SpaceX has caught Super Heavy on three Starship flights to date, but it has never tried the maneuver with Ship. It's a taller order; Ship flies higher and farther than Super Heavy, so its return to Earth is more complex and energetic. SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk already told us that Flight 15 would likely feature a double-catch attempt . But the newly released mission description gives us a launch date, as well as details about the flight. Starship Die Cast Rocket Model Was $47.99 Now $39.99 on Amazon . Even if you can't see SpaceX's Starship in person, you can score a model of your own. Standing at 13.77 inches (35 cm), this is a 1:375 ratio of SpaceX's Starship as a desktop model. The materials here are alloy steel and it weighs just 225g. View Deal Flight 15 is scheduled to launch from Starbase on Friday during a 75-minute window that opens at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT; 4:45 p.m. local Texas time). Super Heavy will come back to Starbase for its tower catch about 6.5 minutes after liftoff, if all goes to plan. But Ship will stay up quite a bit longer. The upper stage will go orbital, something Starship did for the first time on Flight 14 on Sept. 28. And, as on Flight 14, Ship will deploy 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 satellites, the vanguard of a new megaconstellation that will eventually consist of about 100,000 spacecraft , according to Musk. Composite photo showing the Super Heavy booster of SpaceX's Starship megarocket coming in for a landing on the launch mount during the vehicle's fifth-ever test flight, on Oct. 13, 2024. (Image credit: SpaceX via X) But Ship should stay aloft for much longer on Flight 15 than it did on Flight 14, which ended with a splashdown in the northern Pacific Ocean about three hours after liftoff. item.content:encoded: null SpaceX will make spaceflight history this week, if all goes according to plan. "If successful, this will mark the first full recovery of an orbital launch system and a breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket." SpaceX's Starship megarocket launches on its 14th test flight on Sept. 28, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX) Super Heavy is Starship's giant booster, and Starship (or Ship for short) is its upper-stage spacecraft. As SpaceX's description noted, both elements are designed to be fully and rapidly reusable. SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk already told us that Flight 15 would likely feature a double-catch attempt . But the newly released mission description gives us a launch date, as well as details about the flight. Starship Die Cast Rocket Model Was $47.99 Now $39.99 on Amazon . Even if you can't see SpaceX's Starship in person, you can score a model of your own. Standing at 13.77 inches (35 cm), this is a 1:375 ratio of SpaceX's Starship as a desktop model. The materials here are alloy steel and it weighs just 225g. View Deal Flight 15 is scheduled to launch from Starbase on Friday during a 75-minute window that opens at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT; 4:45 p.m. local Texas time). Super Heavy will come back to Starbase for its tower catch about 6.5 minutes after liftoff, if all goes to plan. But Ship will stay up quite a bit longer. The upper stage will go orbital, something Starship did for the first time on Flight 14 on Sept. 28. And, as on Flight 14, Ship will deploy 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 satellites, the vanguard of a new megaconstellation that will eventually consist of about 100,000 spacecraft , according to Musk. Composite photo showing the Super Heavy booster of SpaceX's Starship megarocket coming in for a landing on the launch mount during the vehicle's fifth-ever test flight, on Oct. 13, 2024. (Image credit: SpaceX via X) But Ship should stay aloft for much longer on Flight 15 than it did on Flight 14, which ended with a splashdown in the northern Pacific Ocean about three hours after liftoff. "Starship’s initial return to launch site mission is expected to orbit the Earth at an altitude of ~275 km [171 miles] and complete approximately 14 orbits around the planet over the course of a more than 22-hour flight," SpaceX wrote in its description of Flight 15. "Similar to Starship’s first orbital mission, the flight profile has been designed with the opportunity to insert into a passively safe suborbital trajectory or safely deorbit at multiple pre-determined areas over the ocean after raising to an orbital altitude," the company added. So there's no guarantee that Ship will indeed come back to Starbase for a catch on Flight 15; SpaceX will call off the try if anything is amiss. Whatever happens, however, you should definitely tune in. It's not every day, after all, that you can watch a rocket the size of a 40-story building take flight.

item.title: History in Morocco! How Nigeria’s Flamingos Won the World Cup
item.description: The Flamingos celebrate on stage with green and white confetti as they lift the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup trophy. History was made in Rabat as the Flamingos of Nigeria conquered global football at the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup. Under head coach Akeem Busari , the team executed an extraordinary seven-match campaign at the finals, overcoming an early setback to claim six consecutive victories and become the first African nation to lift any FIFA women’s international trophy. Midfielder Oluebube Umejiaku earned individual recognition by winning the FIFA Golden Ball as the Player of the Tournament alongside Player of the Match honors in the final. The squad also displayed exceptional attacking breadth, scoring goals through eight different players across seven matches at the finals while registering over 100 goal attempts. Oluebube Umejiaku poses with the FIFA Golden Ball and Player of the Match awards following Nigeria’s World Cup triumph. Here is the match-by-match breakdown of how Nigeria navigated the African qualifiers, powered through the World Cup group stage, defeated multi-time global champions in the knockouts, and clinched the ultimate trophy in Morocco. Nigeria’s Flamingos celebrate becoming the first African nation to win the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup after defeating Japan 2-1 in Rabat. Phase 1: The African Qualifying Journey Nigeria entered the African U-17 World Cup qualifying campaign in the second round, establishing dominance in home-and-away aggregate ties across West Africa. The Flamingos opened their qualification run with an emphatic 5–0 away victory in Guinea, led by team captain Harmony Chidi ’s first-half hat-trick alongside goals from Oluwakemi Adegbuyi and Mary Dunstan . They followed up with a 7–0 victory in the home leg in Ogun State to complete a 12–0 aggregate shutout. The Flamingos celebrate on the pitch following their matchday four fixture at the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup. In the final qualifying round, Nigeria established a three-goal lead in Monrovia by defeating Liberia 4–1, thanks to a brace from Harmony Chidi and goals from Shakirat Moshood and Peace Effiong . Chidi then sealed a 2–0 second-leg win back home to finish the qualifiers with 12 goals and secure Nigeria’s ticket to Morocco. Phase 2: Group B at the World Cup (Morocco) Placed in Group B alongside Poland, Puerto Rico, and defending world champions DPR Korea, Nigeria had to battle through one of the tournament’s most competitive pools. The campaign started with a tight 2–1 loss to Poland in Rabat, putting pressure on the team to perform in their remaining fixtures. The Flamingos bounced back immediately with a 2–0 shutout victory over Puerto Rico to claim their first three points. Nigeria’s Flamingos celebrate their historic 3-1 Group B victory over defending champions DPR Korea in Morocco. In their final group match, Nigeria produced one of the tournament’s biggest tactical upsets by defeating two-time defending champions DPR Korea

Goals from Oluwakemi Adegbuyi , Oluebube Umejiaku , and Kanyinsola Yusuf snapped DPR Korea’s long unbeaten regulation-time streak at the U-17 World Cup and sent Nigeria through to the knockouts at the top of Group B on head-to-head tiebreakers. FIFA President Gianni Infantino presents the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup trophy to Nigeria captain Harmony Chidi alongside CAF President Patrice Motsepe. Phase 3: The Knockout Stages Nigeria entered the expanded 16-team knockout rounds, defeating top-tier opponents from CONCACAF, CONMEBOL, and AFC. In the Round of 16, Nigeria put together a strong performance against Mexico, winning 2–1 through goals from Oluebube Umejiaku and Mary Dunstan. The quarter-final against Venezuela proved to be a tense affair, remaining scoreless until the 89th minute when Oluebube Umejiaku won a late penalty. Nigeria captain Harmony Chidi in action during the Round of 16 as the Flamingos secured a 2-1 victory over Mexico in Morocco Substitute defender Azeezat Oduntan converted from the spot to send Nigeria to the semi-finals. Facing South American champions Brazil in Rabat, Nigeria broke through in the 56th minute with a strike from Queen Joseph before forward Awawu Bashiru scored twice in the 71st and 80th minutes to lock in a 3–1 win and book Nigeria’s place in the final. The Final: Nigeria 2–1 Japan Played at the Mohammed VI Football Complex in Rabat, Morocco, Nigeria claimed the World Cup title with a 2–1 victory over Japan. Awawu Bashiru opened the scoring in the 39th minute with a long-range shot. Two minutes after half-time, tournament MVP Oluebube Umejiaku doubled the advantage. Japan pulled a goal back through Fuki Ito in the 80th minute, but Nigeria defended their lead through stoppage time to secure the World Cup trophy. Nigeria’s Flamingos celebrate becoming the first African nation to win the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup after defeating Japan 2-1 in Rabat. The Flamingos react after earning a spot in the quarter-finals of the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup. Nigeria’s Flamingos celebrate on the field following their quarter-final win over Venezuela. *** Photo Credit: FIFA Women’s World Cup/Instagram The post History in Morocco! How Nigeria’s Flamingos Won the World Cup appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: Meteorite that landed in Cape Cod was a 'lone wolf' from the outer solar system, scientists find
item.description: Thanks to a combination of radar, infrasound, dash-cam and security camera footage, astronomers have tracked the bright daytime meteor that fell over Cape Cod Bay in May 2026 back to its origin as a small asteroid perturbed by Jupiter and sent on a comet-like orbit towards Earth. Meteor fireballs visible in the daytime are referred to as 'bolides'. At 1:06 p.m. local time (18:06 UTC) on May 30, 2026 one such bolide was widely witnessed falling out of the sky over coastal Massachusetts, with members of the public also reporting an associated sonic boom that rumbled across the north-eastern coast of the United States. Now, a team of scientists from Europe and the United States, led by space physicist Juha Vierinen of the Arctic University of Norway in Tromsø, have patched together measurements from a meteor-observing radar network, regular weather radar, infrasound stations and camera footage to fully characterize the fall of this meteoroid and trace its orbit around the sun . Key to these observations were measurements by the Spread Spectrum Interferometric Meteor Observing Network (SIMONe) based at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology's (MIT's) Haystack Observatory. SIMONe is a project jointly developed by MIT, the Arctic University of Norway and the Leibniz Institute of Atmospheric Physics in Kühlungsborn, Germany. "We were fortunate that the event occurred within the coverage of SIMONe," Vierinen told Space.com. This is echoed by Ryan Volz, a radio scientist at Haystack Observatory who is a member of the team who studied the May 30 bolide. "We got pretty lucky to observe this one," Volz told Space.com. "A bolide like this would have to enter the atmosphere within about 62 miles (100 kilometers) of a SIMONe-like meteor radar system for the head echoes we saw to be detectable, and there are only a handful of places in the world that currently meet that criteria." A head echo is what radar sees when a meteoroid – what we call the lump of rock that becomes a meteor while it is still in space – enters Earth's atmosphere , generating a cloud of plasma around it as it superheats the atmosphere and its outer surface. "The head echoes give the best constraints on the meteoroid's trajectory," said Volz. The existence of the head echo is usually very brief, taking place at 56 miles (90 kilometers () altitude down to about 44 miles (71 kilometers) when the plasma around the meteoroid is dense enough to return a radar echo. The head echo transitions into a 'trail echo', which is produced by a streak of turbulent plasma that is left in the wake of the meteoroid after it has passed through a given part of the atmosphere. In the case of the 30 May bolide, the trail echo was detected down to an unusually low altitude of 20 miles (32 kilometers), at which point the falling rock fragmented with an explosive force equivalent to 500 tons of TNT, whereas the total impact energy of the bolide was in the region on 1.1 kilotons of TNT. item.dc:creator: Keith Cooper
item.content:encoded: Thanks to a combination of radar, infrasound, dash-cam and security camera footage, astronomers have tracked the bright daytime meteor that fell over Cape Cod Bay in May 2026 back to its origin as a small asteroid perturbed by Jupiter and sent on a comet-like orbit towards Earth. Meteor fireballs visible in the daytime are referred to as 'bolides'. At 1:06 p.m. local time (18:06 UTC) on May 30, 2026 one such bolide was widely witnessed falling out of the sky over coastal Massachusetts, with members of the public also reporting an associated sonic boom that rumbled across the north-eastern coast of the United States. Now, a team of scientists from Europe and the United States, led by space physicist Juha Vierinen of the Arctic University of Norway in Tromsø, have patched together measurements from a meteor-observing radar network, regular weather radar, infrasound stations and camera footage to fully characterize the fall of this meteoroid and trace its orbit around the sun . Key to these observations were measurements by the Spread Spectrum Interferometric Meteor Observing Network (SIMONe) based at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology's (MIT's) Haystack Observatory. SIMONe is a project jointly developed by MIT, the Arctic University of Norway and the Leibniz Institute of Atmospheric Physics in Kühlungsborn, Germany. "We were fortunate that the event occurred within the coverage of SIMONe," Vierinen told Space.com. This is echoed by Ryan Volz, a radio scientist at Haystack Observatory who is a member of the team who studied the May 30 bolide. "We got pretty lucky to observe this one," Volz told Space.com. "A bolide like this would have to enter the atmosphere within about 62 miles (100 kilometers) of a SIMONe-like meteor radar system for the head echoes we saw to be detectable, and there are only a handful of places in the world that currently meet that criteria." A head echo is what radar sees when a meteoroid – what we call the lump of rock that becomes a meteor while it is still in space – enters Earth's atmosphere , generating a cloud of plasma around it as it superheats the atmosphere and its outer surface. "The head echoes give the best constraints on the meteoroid's trajectory," said Volz. The existence of the head echo is usually very brief, taking place at 56 miles (90 kilometers () altitude down to about 44 miles (71 kilometers) when the plasma around the meteoroid is dense enough to return a radar echo. The head echo transitions into a 'trail echo', which is produced by a streak of turbulent plasma that is left in the wake of the meteoroid after it has passed through a given part of the atmosphere. In the case of the 30 May bolide, the trail echo was detected down to an unusually low altitude of 20 miles (32 kilometers), at which point the falling rock fragmented with an explosive force equivalent to 500 tons of TNT, whereas the total impact energy of the bolide was in the region on 1.1 kilotons of TNT. Only three recorded bolides around the world had a greater impact energy in the year before (2025), giving an indication of how rare such events are. At this point, four of the Next Generation Weather Radars (NEXRAD) jointly operated by the National Weather Service, the Federal Aviation Administration and the U.S. Air Force took over, recording the debris from the fragmentation as solid chunks of rock fell as meteorites into Cape Cod Bay. The radar detections were supported by infrasound readings of the atmospheric pressure waves resulting from the hypervelocity fall and break-up of the object. These pressure waves can travel hundreds or thousands of kilometers and were picked up by the Elginfield Infrasound Array (ELFO) in Ontario, Canada, as well as by citizen scientists operating their own Raspberry Shake/Boom pressure sensors, which are build-your-own micro-barometers produced by the Raspberry Pi Foundation. "Six citizen-operated sensors jointly constrained the arrival direction," said Vierinen. "Five other single-station detections and ELFO supplied the signal periods used to estimate the energy release. We are grateful to the citizen scientists whose measurements expanded the coverage and helped locate the event." From the data gathered, the team were able to deduce certain properties about the object that fell to Earth over Massachusetts. The meteoroid that entered the atmosphere was about a meter (approximately three feet) across, and based on how deep it penetrated into the atmosphere before fragmenting it must have been a pretty solid body, possibly rich in iron. "We cannot determine its exact history, but we found no association with any known meteor shower ," said Vierinen. Extrapolating its trajectory back into space, the team found that the meteoroid had a comet -like elongated orbit around the sun that took it almost as far out as Jupiter . Comets on such orbits are referred to as Jupiter-family comets, since their orbits are governed by perturbations from Jupiter's powerful gravitational influence. However, the meteoroid was definitely not a comet, and previous research has found that Jupiter can draw out small asteroids from the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter and place them on such orbits. "Meteoroids can be perturbed by other bodies including Jupiter," team-member Marc Fries told Space.com. "The meteoroid's aphelion – the point where it is farthest from the sun – is close to Jupiter's orbit, which suggests a close pass by the gas giant may have indeed flung it into its recent Earth-crossing path. This same process has slowly depopulated the asteroid belt throughout the solar system 's history." An illustration of our solar system's main asteroid belt, found between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter. (Image credit: NASA) Meteoroids on meter-sized scales are in something of a black spot – they are not very easy to detect in space from Earth unlike larger asteroids, and they are not common enough to be falling to Earth all the time unlike the pebble-sized meteoroids and smaller that burn up as shooting stars. As such, we know relatively little about this population of bodies and every bolide that we see helps us to learn more. "Every new piece of data we glean about Earth impactors adds to the statistics," said Fries. "It is especially helpful to have measurements of total power, location, originating orbit and similar data points for the more massive meteorites, because those are the meteoroids and asteroids we encounter less frequently." That the meteoroid fell over such a highly populated area was a stroke of luck. Although the atmosphere is carefully monitored on a global basis by both ground stations and satellites high above us, meaning that even if a meteor streaks above an uninhabited area there is usually enough data to narrow down its trajectory somewhat, radar observations are able to do so more accurately. "We would love to have global coverage with meteor radar networks and we and others are making progress with SIMONe and similar systems, but the current coverage is still sparse," said Volz. Nevertheless, the Cape Cod bolide resoundingly shows that by combining radar echoes from head and trail plasma with weather radar observations and ultrasound pulses from the break-up of falling rocks, scientists can ascertain the orbits of impacting meteoroids very accurately. While the Cape Cod meteoroid was much smaller than the asteroid that exploded over Chelyabinsk in 2013, which was about 18 meters across and exploded with an energy equivalent to between 400 and 500 kilotons of TNT, being able to trace meteoroids back to their orbits may in future reveal new populations of potentially hazardous impactors. The research into the Cape Cod bolide is available as a preprint on the arXiv server .

item.title: NASA unveils $10 billion in moon base contracts, new lunar missions and the 'PROMISE' of a nuclear-powered rover
item.description: null CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. — NASA is pushing ahead with its plan to build a moon base for astronauts by 2032, with the agency unveiling up to $10 billion in contracts to launch and deliver cargo to the moon and other efforts on Saturday (Nov. 7). The NASA announcement, revealed here during the space agency's "Max Power" air show event at Kennedy Space Center , included plans for a new $10 billion Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) framework, dubbed CLPS 2, about$1.3 billion in funding for the agency's Venture-Class Acquisition of Dedicated and Rideshare (VADR) program, and the nuclear-powered "PROMISE" rover on the moon. The announcements mark another step in NASA's effort to establish infrastructure on the moon before Artemis astronauts return to its surface, including a rover and other cargo and research elements. "Under the current CLPS contract, it's all all or nothing, which might be fine if you're only doing one or two of those [missions] per year," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman told Space.com during a press conference on Saturday. "But when you're trying to scale up to what we're talking about today, you want to have the flexibility to move pieces around." Landing cargo on the moon NASA selected eight companies to compete for the new CLPS 2 missions under the framework: Blue Origin , Firefly Aerospace, Intuitive Machines, ispace-U.S., Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, SpaceX and Voyager Technologies. The contracts for the 10-year CLPS 2 architecture carry a combined maximum value of $10 billion, rather than $10 billion in immediately awarded missions. NASA also increased the ceiling of its existing CLPS contract from $2.6 billion to $4.2 billion to support the agency's "Phase One" Moon Base objectives. NASA is also following through on a promise Isaacman made in June, when he proposed repurposing an engineering model of the Perseverance and Curiosity Mars rovers (essentially an Earth-based twin) as a mission-ready rover to send to the moon. That rover, called PROMISE (short for "Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration"), is a nuclear-powered robot intended to explore the lunar south pole beginning in late 2028. The autonomous rover will carry a drill and scientific instruments to search for volatiles and water ice on the lunar surface. NASA awarded Blue Origin a $94 million base contract, with an additional $140 million option period based on performance, to deliver PROMISE to the lunar surface aboard its Blue Moon Mark 1 lander . Communication satellites, navigation tests and more In addition to that contract for Blue Origin, NASA awarded six launch and orbital transportation task orders worth a total of approximately $1.3 billion to Arrow Science and Technology, Blue Origin and Impulse Space under its Venture-Class Acquisition of Dedicated and Rideshare (VADR) program. The missions will demonstrate commercial launch and orbital transportation capabilities, including cargo transfers between Earth and lunar

"But when you're trying to scale up to what we're talking about today, you want to have the flexibility to move pieces around." NASA also increased the ceiling of its existing CLPS contract from $2.6 billion to $4.2 billion to support the agency's "Phase One" Moon Base objectives. NASA is also following through on a promise Isaacman made in June, when he proposed repurposing an engineering model of the Perseverance and Curiosity Mars rovers (essentially an Earth-based twin) as a mission-ready rover to send to the moon. The autonomous rover will carry a drill and scientific instruments to search for volatiles and water ice on the lunar surface. NASA awarded Blue Origin a $94 million base contract, with an additional $140 million option period based on performance, to deliver PROMISE to the lunar surface aboard its Blue Moon Mark 1 lander . Communication satellites, navigation tests and more In addition to that contract for Blue Origin, NASA awarded six launch and orbital transportation task orders worth a total of approximately $1.3 billion to Arrow Science and Technology, Blue Origin and Impulse Space under its Venture-Class Acquisition of Dedicated and Rideshare (VADR) program. The missions will demonstrate commercial launch and orbital transportation capabilities, including cargo transfers between Earth and lunar orbits, navigation tests with the CAPSTONE 2 spacecraft and lunar scouting with "MoonFall" drones . Blue Origin, SpaceX and Relativity Space will provide launch support with their New Glenn , Falcon 9 and Terran R rockets, respectively. Under a separate lunar logistics contract, NASA selected SpaceX to launch communications satellites aboard its Starship megarocket in 2028, helping to establish a future lunar communications network with spacecraft similar to the company's Starlink spacecraft. NASA also awarded contracts to Honeybee Robotics, Redwire and Yank Technologies to develop components for a lunar power and communications tower, known as miniCAST. The announcements support NASA's Phase One Moon Base strategy, which is scheduled to extend through 2029 and focuses on robotic exploration, infrastructure demonstrations and commercial deliveries. Phase Two, which runs from 2029 to 2032, will continue to build out infrastructure for the base, which will get up and running during Phase 3.

item.title: NASA chief Jared Isaacman skydives into space agency's MAX POWER air show — 'Going into this job, I knew we had to do something like this.'
item.description: null CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. — NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman knows how to make an entrance. Under the bright afternoon sun on Saturday (Nov. 7), Isaacman plummeted through the air above 10,000 onlookers, skydiving into the agency's air show MAX POWER. MAX POWER overtook NASA's Kennedy Space Center here over the weekend, combining aeronautics and aerospace in a massive public air show, the first of its kind for the space agency. A mix of astronauts, fighter jet displays and new technology on display, the spectacle is a lot space-ier than a traditional air show, and Isaacman made sure to really showcase this merging of worlds. A pilot and private astronaut, Jared Isaacman is no stranger to the skies, and immediately after landing back on solid ground he jumped right back up and took to the event's main stage to greet an excited crowd. "Going into this job, I I knew we had to do something like this," Isaacman said after landing and taking the stage. "We knew on our nation's 250th birthday , we had to open up [the] Kennedy Space Center the year that we returned our astronauts to the lunar environment and put on a little bit of a show." NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman parachutes to Earth with members of the Chicago Skydive team. Space.com’s super zoomed-in photo of this jump was made possible by a Canon R5 Mark II camera , with an RF 200-800mm lens. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner) EOS R5 Mark II: $3999 This mirrorless Canon has specs that make it one of the best cameras available right now, with impressive features and functionality, including a 45MP sensor and excellent high-ISO handling. Check our in-depth Canon R5 Mark II review . View Deal And put on a show he did. From thousands of feet above a crowd holding their breath, Isaacman jumped out of a plane alongside members of Skydive Chicago and other notable individuals, including Montana senator Tim Sheehy (R-Montana) and former U.S. Air Force Thunderbird pilot Shawn Gustoson. One by one, tiny white parachutes popped up in the sky above, which continued to grow in size as the skydivers neared the ground. And before we knew it, Isaacman was gracefully touching down just behind the air show's main stage, landing to the sound of cheers from the eager audience. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman jumps out of an airplane with members of the Chicago Skydive team. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner) In addition to serving in his role as NASA Administrator, Isaacman is an entrepreneur, commercial astronaut and pilot. item.dc:creator: Chelsea Gohd
item.content:encoded: null CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. — NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman knows how to make an entrance. Under the bright afternoon sun on Saturday (Nov. 7), Isaacman plummeted through the air above 10,000 onlookers, skydiving into the agency's air show MAX POWER. MAX POWER overtook NASA's Kennedy Space Center here over the weekend, combining aeronautics and aerospace in a massive public air show, the first of its kind for the space agency. A mix of astronauts, fighter jet displays and new technology on display, the spectacle is a lot space-ier than a traditional air show, and Isaacman made sure to really showcase this merging of worlds. A pilot and private astronaut, Jared Isaacman is no stranger to the skies, and immediately after landing back on solid ground he jumped right back up and took to the event's main stage to greet an excited crowd. "Going into this job, I I knew we had to do something like this," Isaacman said after landing and taking the stage. "We knew on our nation's 250th birthday , we had to open up [the] Kennedy Space Center the year that we returned our astronauts to the lunar environment and put on a little bit of a show." NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman parachutes to Earth with members of the Chicago Skydive team. Space.com’s super zoomed-in photo of this jump was made possible by a Canon R5 Mark II camera , with an RF 200-800mm lens. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner) EOS R5 Mark II: $3999 This mirrorless Canon has specs that make it one of the best cameras available right now, with impressive features and functionality, including a 45MP sensor and excellent high-ISO handling. Check our in-depth Canon R5 Mark II review . View Deal And put on a show he did. From thousands of feet above a crowd holding their breath, Isaacman jumped out of a plane alongside members of Skydive Chicago and other notable individuals, including Montana senator Tim Sheehy (R-Montana) and former U.S. Air Force Thunderbird pilot Shawn Gustoson. One by one, tiny white parachutes popped up in the sky above, which continued to grow in size as the skydivers neared the ground. And before we knew it, Isaacman was gracefully touching down just behind the air show's main stage, landing to the sound of cheers from the eager audience. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman jumps out of an airplane with members of the Chicago Skydive team. (Image credit: Space.com / Josh Dinner) In addition to serving in his role as NASA Administrator, Isaacman is an entrepreneur, commercial astronaut and pilot. Known in flight by his callsign "Rook" which he was given during fighter jet training, Isaacman has so far logged over 8,000 flight hours. In 2009, he broke the world record for fastest trip around the world in a light jet (he made the trip in 61 hours, 51 minutes and 15 seconds) and is flight-qualified in a number of military jet aircraft. He also financed and flew on two private orbital space missions on a SpaceX Dragon, Inspiration4 and Polaris Dawn , performing the world's first private spacewalk on the latter misison. Before jumping out of a plane and careening through the air on Saturday as part of this celebratory stunt, Isaacman was actually flying overhead in not one, but two different fighter jets. First, he flew an F-5, a lightweight supersonic fighter jet, and just a short while later, Isaacman flew a MiG-29, a twin-engine supersonic fighter jet, over the crowd of excited air show attendees. And the fun didn't stop with this skydive, as Isaacman took to the skies once again, flying over the event in fighter jets on Sunday. How do you follow this act? This weekend's MAX POWER events are not a one-time-only celebration of aviation and aerospace at NASA. Earlier in the weekend, the agency announced that in 2028, a week-long event called CAPEWEEK will return to the Kennedy Space Center, promising a next-level showcase of air and space innovation and spectacle. Isaacman and NASA astronauts presented President Donald Trump, who was onhand for the ceremony , with a gold plaque in his honor that will be installed at the Kennedy Space Center's Shuttle Landing Facility runway in time for the CAPEWEEK in 2028. "What you are seeing today again, imagine March 2028," Isaacman said of the future. "It's going to be 10x bigger. I mean, not just the the fighter aircraft you're seeing, but displays of aerospace-related hardware, rovers, landers. We're going to bring commercial airliners in here ... I would bet on this, the next new Grand Airliner will be announced here." "That kind of ambition is exactly that you should expect from your space agency," he added. "I promise you, there'll be more to come."

item.title: AOT Lagos 8.0 Returns with Bold Focus on AI, Ethics and Digital Governance
item.description: As Africa accelerates its digital transformation journey, the conversation is no longer simply about adopting new technologies, it is now about ensuring they are deployed responsibly, governed effectively, and trusted by the people they serve. It is against this backdrop that the Eko Innovation Centre, in collaboration with the Lagos State Ministry of Innovation, Science & Technology, announces the 8th edition of the Art of Technology Lagos (AOT Lagos 8.0) , scheduled to hold on Thursday, 3 December 2026, at the Landmark Event Centre, Victoria Island, Lagos. Now in its eighth year, AOT Lagos has welcomed over 125,000 participants, hosted 340 speakers, delivered 262 keynote sessions, and generated more than 15 million engagements across 145 countries. More importantly, AOT Lagos has evolved beyond a conference into a platform for collaboration and policy development, contributing to landmark initiatives including the Lagos Innovation Master Plan, Startup Lagos, the Talent Acceleration Masterplan, the Lagos Digital Service Portal, and the Lagos Digital Service Portal 2.0 (Chatbot Inclusive). This year’s theme, “Beyond Smart Cities: Tech Adoption × Ethics × Governance,” reflects one of the defining conversations of our time. As artificial intelligence, digital public infrastructure, connected services, and data-driven technologies continue to transform economies and societies, governments and businesses must ensure innovation is underpinned by transparency, accountability, inclusion, and public trust. Bringing these critical conversations to the forefront, AOT Lagos 8.0 will feature a distinguished line-up of technology leaders, policymakers, entrepreneurs, and global industry experts , including Dr. Bosun Tijani , the Honourable Minister of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy, Sade Dada , Head of Public Policy, Anglophone West Africa at Meta, Engr. Abisoye Coker-Odusote, Director-General and Chief Executive Officer of the National Identity Management Commission (NIMC), the Honourable Commissioner, Ministry of Innovation, Science and Technology, Lagos State Olatubosun Alake and more. Their participation will bring diverse perspectives to the conference’s central conversations around responsible AI adoption, digital governance, smart infrastructure, the future of work, digital inclusion, and sustainable innovation. Speaking on this year’s edition, Victor Afolab i, Founder of Eko Innovation Centre, said: “Technology is changing faster than ever before, but sustainable progress depends on more than innovation alone. It requires responsible adoption, effective governance, and meaningful collaboration across the public and private sectors. AOT Lagos 8.0 provides a platform for the conversations, partnerships, and ideas that will help shape Africa’s digital future .” This year’s conference will feature executive keynotes, policy dialogues, ministerial roundtables, technology exhibitions, startup showcases, investment engagements, and strategic

AOT Lagos 8.0 provides a platform for the conversations, partnerships, and ideas that will help shape Africa’s digital future .” This year’s conference will feature executive keynotes, policy dialogues, ministerial roundtables, technology exhibitions, startup showcases, investment engagements, and strategic conversations across eight thematic tracks covering: AI, Ethics & Governance Smart Infrastructure & Urban Innovation Fintech, Regulation & Digital Economy Future of Work & Talent Transformation Digital Identity, Data & Cybersecurity ClimateTech & Sustainable Cities Civic Technology & Digital Inclusion Startup Innovation & Investment The conference will also host the 5th AOT Ecosystem Awards , recognising outstanding startups, ecosystem builders, policymakers, and organisations driving innovation and digital transformation across Nigeria and the African continent. Building on seven successful editions, AOT Lagos 8.0 aims to strengthen public-private collaboration, inspire innovative solutions, encourage investment, and generate policy recommendations that support responsible technology adoption and sustainable digital transformation across Africa. To learn more or register to attend, visit www.aotlagos.com . item.title: Israel Olaleye: What Selling Land Taught Me About How Nigerians Think About Money
item.description: In 2021, I graduated from the University of Ibadan with a degree in Mathematics. I thought my life would be about numbers on a whiteboard. I did not know it would become about numbers in people’s bank accounts, and the fears, hopes and contradictions that sit behind them. By mid-2023, I had taken a job selling real estate. I started at the very bottom, as a sales development representative: the person who makes the first call, sends the message and follows up when nobody replies. Today, I manage a sales team. Somewhere between then and now, I stopped seeing real estate as a business of land and buildings. I started seeing it as a mirror. Put a property in front of a Nigerian, and you will learn, very quickly, how they think about money. Here is some of what that mirror has shown me: A prospect once told me, with complete confidence, “I have my money ready for the land.” We fixed an inspection. We walked the site together under the afternoon sun, red earth on our shoes. Then, standing on the plot, the prospect asked if they could pay next year. I was not angry. I understood. Saying “I am ready” feels good. Being ready is different. It means you have decided what the money is for, and you are willing to let it go. I have seen versions of that moment many times. The client who books an inspection for 2 pm and is still not there at 4 pm. The person who asks for options, receives ten properties that match exactly what they requested, and replies, “Do you have something else?” The buyer who is ready until it is time to decide, and then needs three more months to think. The one who disappeared after asking for a price came back after the price went up, and asked for the old price. For a long time, these moments frustrated me. But they taught me that most people do not have a money problem. They have a decision problem. We are a generation that earns, spends, plans and postpones, often all at the same time. You can earn a lot and still not be wealthy One idea I keep returning to is that you can earn twenty million naira a year and still not be wealthy. Income is what comes in. Wealth is what stays and grows. Two people can earn the same salary and end up in completely different places ten years later, simply because one converted part of that income into assets and the other converted all of it into lifestyle. Wealthy people do not always look wealthy. Some of the most financially secure people I have met do not drive the loudest cars. And some of the people who look the richest are one bad month away from panic. So the question I now ask myself, and the people I speak with, is simple: what exactly are you converting your income into? item.dc:creator: Israel Toluwalope Olaleye
item.content:encoded: In 2021, I graduated from the University of Ibadan with a degree in Mathematics. I thought my life would be about numbers on a whiteboard. I did not know it would become about numbers in people’s bank accounts, and the fears, hopes and contradictions that sit behind them. By mid-2023, I had taken a job selling real estate. I started at the very bottom, as a sales development representative: the person who makes the first call, sends the message and follows up when nobody replies. Today, I manage a sales team. Somewhere between then and now, I stopped seeing real estate as a business of land and buildings. I started seeing it as a mirror. Put a property in front of a Nigerian, and you will learn, very quickly, how they think about money. Here is some of what that mirror has shown me: A prospect once told me, with complete confidence, “I have my money ready for the land.” We fixed an inspection. We walked the site together under the afternoon sun, red earth on our shoes. Then, standing on the plot, the prospect asked if they could pay next year. I was not angry. I understood. Saying “I am ready” feels good. Being ready is different. It means you have decided what the money is for, and you are willing to let it go. I have seen versions of that moment many times. The client who books an inspection for 2 pm and is still not there at 4 pm. The person who asks for options, receives ten properties that match exactly what they requested, and replies, “Do you have something else?” The buyer who is ready until it is time to decide, and then needs three more months to think. The one who disappeared after asking for a price came back after the price went up, and asked for the old price. For a long time, these moments frustrated me. But they taught me that most people do not have a money problem. They have a decision problem. We are a generation that earns, spends, plans and postpones, often all at the same time. You can earn a lot and still not be wealthy One idea I keep returning to is that you can earn twenty million naira a year and still not be wealthy. Income is what comes in. Wealth is what stays and grows. Two people can earn the same salary and end up in completely different places ten years later, simply because one converted part of that income into assets and the other converted all of it into lifestyle. Wealthy people do not always look wealthy. Some of the most financially secure people I have met do not drive the loudest cars. And some of the people who look the richest are one bad month away from panic. So the question I now ask myself, and the people I speak with, is simple: what exactly are you converting your income into? Real estate is bigger than land and a house One conversation changed how I explain property to people. A Nigerian living in Canada called me after watching a video I had made about a commercial development in Ibadan. A few minutes in, he said something I have since heard from many people: “To me, real estate has always meant two things. You buy land and keep it, or you build a house to live in.” That is how many of us were raised to think about property. Land is pride. A house is security. Both are good. But they are only part of the picture. Some assets are for appreciation. Some assets are for cash flow. Land grows in value while you wait, but it does not pay you while you wait. A shop, a rental apartment or a short-let can pay you while it grows. When I explained this, the whole conversation changed. We stopped talking about a single plot and started talking about a plan. Not long after, I had almost the same conversation with another Nigerian abroad. He had never considered property as something that could produce income. He liked what he heard. He even had a deposit ready. But he planned to buy more than a year later. I had to tell him honestly that the option he liked might not be there by then. The right asset rarely waits for our calendars. Patience is not the same as understanding Another lesson came from buyers who purchase property with a five-year plan and then become anxious when the value has not doubled in eight months. I used to think the answer was simply to tell people to be patient. Now I think the real mistake is not impatience. It is entering an investment without knowing what you are waiting for. Is it a road under construction? A growing population? New businesses moving in? If you do not know what should drive the value, every month of waiting feels like a loss. Don’t just trust. Verify The hardest lesson is about trust. Many Nigerians abroad send money home and leave a relative to handle everything. The intention is love. But love is not a process. Money gets misused. Documents are not checked. Sites are not visited. My advice is never to stop trusting family. It is to stop relying on trust alone. Have a lawyer who checks the title. Have a surveyor who confirms the land. Let family monitor. And yes, check the consultant too, including people like me. Professionals can be dishonest. Don’t just trust. Verify. I would rather a client ask me ten uncomfortable questions before buying than discover after payment that there was something they should have checked. Closing a deal is good. Knowing that the person understood exactly what they were buying is better. What I am building When I started, I thought success in sales would be measured by how many properties I sold. I still care about that. But I care more now about something harder to count: whether the people I speak with make better decisions with their money because of the conversation we had. I want to keep learning, keep growing and keep building something that means more than a sales record. And I will say it plainly, the way I sometimes say it to myself on difficult days: watch out for a few years when you hear my name. Not because I will have sold the most land. But because I hope my name will stand for something many Nigerians are still searching for when it comes to money and property: honest guidance, good judgment and trust that is earned, not assumed. The mirror is still there. Every inspection, every delayed payment, every late-night call from abroad shows me something new. And the biggest thing it has shown me is that before people buy property, they need to understand their own relationship with money. item.title: WSL talking points: Tullis-Joyce takes charge and is Shaw the perfect striker?
item.description: The City forward hit a WSL hat-trick for the ninth time while Eva Olid’s United have found defensive stability Not only did Khadija “Bunny” Shaw score a record-extending ninth WSL hat-trick, she scored a “perfect hat-trick” for the fourth time in the competition, something nobody else has managed more than once. Against West Ham the Jamaica striker opened the scoring with her left foot, headed home her second off the underside of the crossbar and tucked in her third with her right foot late on. It helped her side towards a 5-0 win that opened up a two-point gap at the top of the table and stretched Shaw’s lead in the race to be the top division’s top scorer to a five-goal advantage over her nearest challenger, Océane Hurtré. Can anybody stop her relentless pursuit of another Golden Boot? It would appear not. Tom Garry Match report: Liverpool 1-2 Arsenal Continue reading...

item.title: Yes, it runs 'Doom': Satellite plays iconic game in world's 1st demonstration of orbital voice control
item.description: null A satellite went knee-deep in the dead, after a voice command from the ground activated the Doom video game in space. Playing a first-person shooter from 1993 was obviously not in the design plan for the PRETTY cubesat , which is run by a consortium including the European Space Agency (ESA). But the pioneering voice command opens up new worlds for satellite work, the team says. "Someone in distress at sea or in a remote area could transmit 'mayday' or "help" on a radio," stated Estonia's Tanagra Space, which supplied the software for the feat. The hope is one day, a satellite could use transcription and AI to alert rescue services for assisting folks in remote zones. The call to play Doom, thankfully, had no other urgency than curiosity — and teamwork, fueled by pizza. OPS-SAT Space Lab managed the experiment on behalf of ESA. Radio amateurs then made six unsuccessful attempts during passes over Poland and Norway, between April and July. The seventh finally reached success under the Oslo Group of the Norwegian Radio Relay League. "We are radio amateurs, with the emphasis on amateurs. Satellite work was not something our club did, and we had no budget for it," representative Eskil Hadland, call sign LB6AJ, said in the Tangara statement. "So we borrowed a line wrongly credited to Pippi Longstocking: 'I have never tried that before, so I should definitely be able to do that.'" The Norwegians spent 59 days and about 7200 NOK or $775 (pizza included) to reach PRETTY, helping make changes to the satellite software to pick up a voice. For example, a raw recording of an attempt on July 3, retransmitted to Earth, showed the spoken words to space were unrecognizable. Further work revealed the satellite's receiver channel was too wide to pick up the voice signal, leading to a fix to narrow the channel. The historic voice command on July 27— in part, "PRETTY play Doom Doom Doom"— came from a rooftop in Oslo, and was spoken at night by Jon Bergli Heier (LB9BJ). PRETTY picked up the transmission, transcribed the command using on-board voice recognition, and then — just like a typical evening gamer—opened up Doom for a play session. A member of the LB9BJ team speaks the command that activated Doom on the OPS-SAT PRETTY satellite while on a rooftop in Oslo, Norway during an evening pass of the spacecraft on July 27, 2026. (Image credit: Truls Johansen (LA7IJ), LA4O) This was no multiplayer gaming situation, but the satellite did create a report of its demon-slaying skills — and its ability to interpret the command. For example, PRETTY generated a "postcard" including a frame of the gameplay, a transcription, and signal diagnostics. The satellite also transmitted its recording of Hadland's command. As anybody who uses voice-recognition software knows, there are challenges in transcriptions: nobody speaks in exactly the same way, and aspects such as accent or background noise can lead to misinterpretations. The satellite also had to contend with Doppler shift
